Apache warns of Roller RCE vulnerability exploited in attacks

Apache warns that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-129448, a critical unauthenticated deserialization flaw in Apache Roller that enables remote code execution. Organizations should upgrade to Roller 6.1.6 or later immediately, or apply the documented XML-RPC mitigations.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Apache has released security updates for CVE-2026-129448, a critical Apache Roller flaw that is being actively exploited in attacks.
  • 02The flaw affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to run arbitrary code because the XML-RPC endpoint processes certain data before verifying the requester.
  • 03Apache recommends upgrading immediately to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the affected extension types and rejects malicious XML-RPC requests.
  • 04Organizations unable to upgrade immediately can mitigate the issue by disabling extensions, removing the XML-RPC servlet mapping, and restarting Roller.
  • 05Disabling XML-RPC through Roller’s administration interface alone does not prevent attacks because vulnerable versions process the request before checking that setting.

Apache has released security updates for CVE-2026-129448, a critical flaw in Apache Roller that the organization says is being actively exploited. Apache Roller is an open-source, Java-based group-blogging server. Apache has not disclosed who is conducting the attacks or how many servers have been compromised.

The flaw affects Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. Roller’s XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and processes them before authenticating the requester. Apache recommends upgrading to Roller 6.1.6 or later; organizations unable to update can apply configuration changes that disable extensions and remove the XML-RPC servlet mapping, then restart Roller.

  • Turning off XML-RPC in Roller’s administration interface is insufficient because vulnerable versions deserialize XML-RPC requests before checking whether the feature is enabled.
  • The issue was previously tracked as CVE-2026-82384, which identified only Roller 6.1.5 as affected, while the updated advisory identifies versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4.
  • For organizations that cannot upgrade immediately, Apache’s workaround requires configuration and servlet-mapping changes followed by a Roller restart.
  • Apache has not disclosed who is behind the ongoing attacks or how many Roller servers have been compromised.

Apache says attackers are actively taking advantage of a serious flaw in its Roller blogging software, which can let an outsider take control of a server without needing to sign in. Organizations that run Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 are affected and should update to version 6.1.6 or later, or use Apache’s temporary workaround. Although Roller is a niche product, a successful break-in could let attackers run their own commands on an organization’s systems, putting data and services at risk.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Apache reports active exploitation of a critical unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw in Apache Roller and provides an immediate upgrade path and temporary mitigations. Roller has a smaller market share than mainstream platforms, which limits the article’s broad relevance, but affected administrators should treat it as urgent.

Microsoft announces Windows Server 2028 with hardened security

Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028, featuring a hardened Server Core configuration and security baseline enabled by default, alongside improved management, NVMe/ReFS storage capabilities, and local AI inference support.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028 at its Ignite 2026 conference as the next major release of its server operating system.
  • 02Windows Server 2028 ships with a hardened Server Core configuration and a new security baseline enabled by default, with options for administrators to relax specific settings.
  • 03The default hardening includes protections for identity, network communications, cryptography, administrator access, code integrity, remote access, and logging.
  • 04Microsoft said it is still working on additional protections, including NTLM blocking, hardware-backed platform protection, and print and RPC hardening.
  • 05Windows Server 2028 adds Intune management for eligible persistent servers, native NVMe storage by default, ReFS boot support, and AI inference tooling for accelerated hardware and custom models.

Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028 at the Ignite 2026 conference as the next major release of its server operating system. The release uses a hardened Server Core configuration by default and introduces a security baseline that administrators can selectively relax. Microsoft said this is intended to reduce the work required to establish a secure configuration from the first day.

The default protections include Kerberos over NTLM, protected LSASS, stronger password and account-lockout policies, SMB signing and encryption, a firewall enabled for all profiles, modern TLS cipher suites, and hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM key exchange. It also includes stricter code-signature validation, encrypted paging files, RDP with Network Level Authentication and TLS, restricted WinRM authentication options, and expanded auditing and logging. Microsoft is still developing additional measures such as NTLM blocking, hardware-backed platform protection, and further print and RPC hardening.

Windows Server 2028 also adds Intune management for eligible persistent servers, providing workflows for configuration, compliance, applications, and updates. Storage and performance changes include native NVMe storage by default, NVMe over TCP and RDMA transports, and booting from ReFS. The release further adds AI capabilities for deploying and configuring inference environments, managing accelerated hardware, and supporting models through Windows ML, Foundry Local, vLLM, and Llama.cpp.

  • Windows Server 2028 reverses the usual setup burden by applying a hardened Server Core configuration from first boot, while allowing administrators to relax individual settings when needed.
  • The default protections span both prevention and visibility: they restrict older or unencrypted connections while also enabling detailed auditing, command-line logging, PowerShell script logging, and larger event logs.
  • Microsoft’s hardening effort is not complete at launch, as NTLM blocking, hardware-backed platform protection, and additional print and RPC protections are still being developed.
  • The release combines server security and administration changes with infrastructure capabilities such as booting from ReFS, native NVMe storage, and management of local AI inference environments.

Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028, a new version of software that organizations use to run many of their internal computer systems and services. It will start with stronger safety settings already turned on, making it harder for criminals or unauthorized people to steal passwords, connect through unsafe network methods, or change important system functions. Organizations that use Windows servers may have less work to do to set up basic protections, while still being able to loosen specific settings when necessary. The release also adds easier large-scale management, faster storage options, and tools for running AI models locally.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Windows Server 2028 is a major Microsoft server-platform release with broad relevance for organizations that run Windows Server. Its default hardened configuration changes authentication, network, cryptography, remote access, and logging settings that administrators may need to evaluate before deployment.

From Deepfakes to Helpdesk Impersonation: Why Stronger Verification Matters

Deepfakes and helpdesk impersonation are making social-engineering attacks more convincing, enabling attackers to trigger fraudulent payments, gain remote access, or reset accounts. Organizations should use strong identity verification, independent confirmation for sensitive actions, and phishing-resistant MFA rather than relying on employees to spot impostors.
KEY POINTS
  • 01An Arup finance employee transferred about HK$200 million (US$25.6 million) after a fake video conference appeared to show the company’s CFO and colleagues requesting transactions.
  • 02Marks & Spencer said attackers gained entry through employees at a third-party contractor, and the April 2025 incident disrupted online orders, payments, Click & Collect services, and exposed customer data.
  • 03Microsoft reported a campaign in which attackers posing as IT support staff used Teams messages or calls to persuade employees to grant remote access through screen sharing or Quick Assist.
  • 04The article recommends stronger identity verification for service-desk and business-workflow requests, as well as independent confirmation for financial transactions, privileged access, and other sensitive actions.

The article examines how deepfakes, helpdesk impersonation, and social engineering can be used to obtain money or access. In January 2024, an Arup finance employee transferred approximately HK\(200 million (US\)25.6 million) after joining a fake video conference that appeared to include the company’s CFO and colleagues. Hong Kong police said attackers used publicly available video and audio to create a convincing pre-recorded conference. In April 2025, Marks & Spencer suffered a major cyberattack after attackers deceived employees at a third-party contractor, disrupting services and resulting in customer-data theft.

Microsoft also reported a campaign in which attackers impersonated IT support personnel through Teams messages or calls and persuaded employees to grant remote access through screen sharing or Quick Assist. Once connected, the attackers used PowerShell to install malicious software, retain access, and gather information about the compromised network, including attempts to move toward domain controllers and certificate authorities. The article argues that employees cannot be expected to identify every convincing impersonation attempt, particularly when attackers use familiar communication channels and conduct reconnaissance. It recommends stronger identity checks for service-desk requests, independent confirmation for sensitive actions such as payments and privileged access, and consistent verification in chatbots and automated workflows.

  • A convincing impersonation does not require a technical flaw in a company’s own systems; the M&S incident involved attackers deceiving staff at a third-party contractor.
  • Routine processes such as password resets and remote support can become entry points when identity checks rely on information that attackers may already have obtained.
  • Employee awareness training alone is not presented as sufficient, because attackers can research targets and make fraudulent requests appear routine.
  • Identity verification can be built into service desks, chatbots, and automated workflows so that the same checks apply across support channels.

The article describes how criminals can pretend to be trusted coworkers or IT support workers, including by using fake video meetings made with copied voices and faces. At engineering firm Arup, this led an employee to send about US$25.6 million, while Marks & Spencer was disrupted after attackers fooled workers at an outside support company. These scams can also trick employees into letting criminals control their computers, putting company systems and customer information at risk. The article argues that companies need reliable ways to confirm a person’s identity before resetting accounts, approving payments, or granting access.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This sponsored article uses several past incidents to illustrate broad identity-verification and social-engineering risks, rather than reporting a new urgent event or technical finding. Its recommendations are generally useful but largely evergreen best practices.

Ukraine, FBI arrest ransomware gang members tied to $40M in ransoms

Ukrainian police and the FBI arrested four suspected members of a multinational ransomware network linked to more than $40.5 million in payments from at least 28 victims. The group allegedly used AI-generated IT-support calls, phishing pages, and remote-access tools to steal data, encrypt systems, and extort companies worldwide.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Ukrainian authorities and the FBI arrested four suspected key members of an international ransomware organization linked to more than $40.5 million in ransom payments from at least 28 companies.
  • 02Investigators said the organization included at least 27 people from Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Russia, and other countries and was connected to a larger network of more than 60 members across eight jurisdictions.
  • 03The group allegedly posed as IT support personnel, using AI-generated voice messages, phishing pages, spoofed phone numbers, and remote-access tools such as TeamViewer and AnyDesk to obtain access to corporate networks.
  • 04Ukrainian court records identify Warren Oil Company, Maxxis International-USA, Newpark Resources, and Quantum Health as victims, with Warren Oil allegedly paying 84.5 BTC, approximately $5 million at the time, after an August 2024 attack.
  • 05Authorities conducted 66 searches in Kyiv and 11 other Ukrainian regions, seized devices, bank cards, nearly $370,000 in cash and €20,000, and said the detained suspects could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.

Ukrainian authorities, working with the FBI, arrested four suspected key members of an international ransomware organization connected to more than $40.5 million in payments from at least 28 companies. Investigators said the wider organization included at least 27 people from Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Russia, and other countries, and was linked to a network of more than 60 members across eight jurisdictions. The group targeted organizations in sectors including oil and gas, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing, logistics, finance, and critical infrastructure.

The suspects allegedly researched victims before stealing company data, locking access to systems, and demanding cryptocurrency in exchange for restoring access and withholding stolen information. To enter corporate networks, they allegedly impersonated IT-support staff through fraudulent calls using AI-generated voices, phishing pages resembling company VPN services, spoofed phone numbers, and remote-access software including TeamViewer and AnyDesk. Ukrainian authorities conducted 66 searches across Kyiv and 11 other regions, seized devices, bank cards, nearly $370,000 in cash and €20,000, and said the detained suspects could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.

  • The group reportedly combined AI-generated support calls with a second attacker working in parallel, keeping an employee on the phone until the attackers confirmed they had entered the company’s systems.
  • Investigators said the criminals researched a target’s finances, assets, employees, and technology weaknesses before attacking, indicating that ransom demands were informed by the victim’s perceived ability to pay.
  • The alleged Warren Oil intrusion shows that obtaining both a worker’s login details and a two-factor authentication code was enough to enable remote access to the corporate network.
  • Although the network was linked to former Conti members and one victim was claimed by BlackSuit, Ukrainian authorities did not confirm that the four arrested people belonged to Conti, BlackSuit, or Chaos.
  • The group’s alleged use of stolen-data publication threats alongside system lockouts put victims under two separate forms of pressure to pay.

Ukraine and the FBI arrested four people suspected of helping run a criminal group that took more than $40.5 million from at least 28 companies around the world. The group allegedly pretended to be company IT staff in phone calls, sometimes using computer-generated voices, to trick workers into sharing passwords or installing software that gave the criminals access. They then stole company files, locked companies out of their own systems, and demanded payment to restore access and avoid publishing the stolen information. The case shows how social deception can disrupt businesses in important sectors such as oil and gas, medicine, manufacturing, transport, finance, and public services.

It also provides actionable detail on the group’s use of AI-generated IT-support impersonation, phishing pages, stolen two-factor codes, and remote-access tools.

Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI package compromised to steal credentials

Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI package was compromised with two malicious releases that automatically stole cloud, CI/CD, and developer credentials during Python startup. Developers who installed versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 should isolate affected systems, rebuild using 1.26.0, and rotate potentially exposed secrets immediately.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI was compromised through malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, published on November 17, 2026.
  • 02The malicious releases used Python startup files to run a credential stealer automatically, including when the Agent Framework package was not imported.
  • 03The stealer targeted secrets in environment variables, local configuration files, and accessible running processes, including credentials for Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI.
  • 04PyPI quarantined the first malicious release, but a second malicious version was published about 2.5 minutes later and quarantined roughly eight minutes afterward.
  • 05Developers who installed either affected version are advised to isolate the environment, rebuild from a known-clean environment using version 1.26.0, and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

Hackers compromised Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and published malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on November 17, 2026. Agent Framework is an open-source toolkit for building and coordinating AI agents, with roughly 200,000 monthly PyPI downloads. The malicious releases contained a credential stealer designed to collect cloud and developer secrets. They retained the legitimate agent-framework-core 1.26.0 dependency, allowing the framework to continue working while the malicious activity ran in the background.

The malicious code executed automatically during normal Python startup through .pth files, including in environments where Agent Framework was not imported. Version 1.26.1 used agent_framework_meta.pth to execute code in agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py, while version 1.26.2 used af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. The stealer sought secrets in environment variables, local configuration files, and accessible running processes, targeting services including Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI. It also attempted to obtain Azure managed identity tokens, Azure DevOps OIDC tokens, and, in version 1.26.2, GitHub Actions OIDC tokens and data from GitHub runner directories.

Both releases sent collected data to the same attacker-controlled webhook endpoint. PyPI quarantined the first release, but another malicious version was uploaded about 2.5 minutes later and was quarantined roughly eight minutes afterward; how the attacker obtained publishing access remains unclear. Developers who installed either version should isolate affected environments, avoid running Python or pip until they are secured, rebuild from a known-clean environment with version 1.26.0, and rotate credentials that may have been exposed. Investigators are advised to search egress logs for the specified webhook path and determine whether attempted transfers were blocked or completed.

  • The malicious packages retained the legitimate agent-framework-core 1.26.0 dependency, allowing the framework to continue functioning normally while credential theft occurred in the background.
  • The credential stealer ran during normal Python startup through .pth files, meaning it could execute even when developers did not import the compromised Agent Framework package.
  • The attacker published a second malicious version about 2.5 minutes after PyPI quarantined the first, showing that the publishing access remained active after the initial response.
  • Investigators can use the specific webhook URL path in outbound network logs to determine whether data theft attempts were blocked or successfully completed.

Hackers put harmful code into two versions of Microsoft’s Agent Framework download for Python, a tool used by many developers to build AI programs. Anyone who installed those versions may have had passwords, access keys, and login tokens for services such as Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, GitHub, Docker, and OpenAI quietly collected and sent to the attackers. This matters because stolen access can let criminals reach company systems and cloud resources beyond the developer’s own computer, so affected users should rebuild their setup and change any exposed credentials.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a high-impact software supply-chain compromise affecting Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package, with roughly 200,000 monthly downloads. The malicious releases automatically harvested cloud and CI/CD credentials during Python startup, creating an immediate need for affected developers and organizations to investigate, rebuild environments, and rotate secrets.

British Scattered Spider hacker sentenced to 6 years in prison

British Scattered Spider leader Tyler Buchanan was sentenced to six years in U.S. prison for phishing employees, conducting SIM-swap-enabled cryptocurrency theft totaling more than $11.6 million, and conspiring to hack multiple companies.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man described as a Scattered Spider leader, was sentenced to six years in U.S. federal prison.
  • 02Buchanan and his accomplices used hundreds of SMS phishing messages impersonating employers or IT and business-process-outsourcing suppliers to obtain employee credentials and personal information.
  • 03The stolen information was used in SIM-swapping attacks to steal more than $11.6 million in cryptocurrency from compromised accounts and wallets.

  • 05Other charged Scattered Spider conspirators, including Noah Michael Urban, have also received multi-year prison sentences.

Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man described as a leader of the Scattered Spider cybercrime collective, was sentenced to six years in U.S. federal prison. He pleaded guilty to cryptocurrency theft charges after prosecutors accused him and four others of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft connected to phishing activity from September 2021 through April 2023. Buchanan was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and has been in U.S. federal custody since April 2025.

The group sent hundreds of fraudulent text messages impersonating victim companies or their IT and business-process-outsourcing suppliers, aiming to collect employee credentials and personal information through lookalike websites. The stolen details were used in SIM-swapping schemes to compromise cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, resulting in more than $11.6 million in stolen virtual currency. The victims included companies in telecommunications, technology, entertainment, outsourcing, IT services, cloud communications, and virtual currency, as well as individual victims; other charged conspirators have also received multi-year prison sentences.

  • The thefts combined fake employee text messages with phone-number takeovers, showing that access to a phone number could be used to reach cryptocurrency accounts and wallets after account information was stolen.
  • A device found at Buchanan’s Scotland residence contained victims’ names, addresses, cryptocurrency recovery phrases, and account login information, indicating that the conspiracy retained highly sensitive data beyond the initial phishing activity.
  • Scattered Spider is described as a loose group that organizes through Telegram, Discord, and hacker forums, rather than as a single formal organization.
  • The group’s activity affected organizations across telecommunications, technology, entertainment, outsourcing, IT services, cloud communications, and virtual-currency services, illustrating its reach across multiple industries.
  • The article says Scattered Spider partnered with BlackCat/AlphV, Qilin, and RansomHub ransomware operations beginning in early 2023.

A British man described as a leader of the Scattered Spider crime group was sentenced to six years in a U.S. prison for helping steal more than $11.6 million in cryptocurrency and break into companies. The group sent fake text messages that appeared to come from employers or their technology providers, tricking workers into giving away account details, and sometimes took over victims’ phone numbers to access cryptocurrency accounts. Companies in telecommunications, technology, entertainment, outsourcing, and IT services, as well as individual cryptocurrency holders, were affected. The case shows how deceptive messages and stolen personal information can lead to major financial losses and serious consequences for victims.

Coinbase blocks $4.7 million in transfers to Elon Musk deepfake scam

Coinbase says its AI fraud-prevention system blocked $4.7 million—about 91% of attempted transfers—to scammers using an Elon Musk deepfake in a fake Tesla livestream to promote a cryptocurrency giveaway.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Scammers used an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk in a fake YouTube livestream resembling Tesla's "flying car" demonstration to promote a cryptocurrency giveaway.
  • 02The fraudulent stream displayed cryptocurrency wallet addresses and a QR code and promised viewers that cryptocurrency they sent would be doubled.
  • 03Coinbase said hundreds of customers attempted to send money to the scammers over roughly two hours, including many longtime exchange users.
  • 04Coinbase said its automated fraud-prevention systems blocked about 91% of attempted transfers, totaling $4.7 million.
  • 05Coinbase's system identified suspicious outgoing transfers and used an AI agent to explain suspected scam signs and ask customers questions before allowing additional safeguards.

Coinbase said it blocked $4.7 million in attempted cryptocurrency transfers to scammers who used an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk during a fake YouTube livestream resembling Tesla’s “flying car” demonstration. The stream showed cryptocurrency wallet addresses and a QR code, telling viewers that any cryptocurrency sent would be doubled. Hundreds of Coinbase customers, including longtime users, attempted to send funds to the scammers over roughly two hours.

Coinbase said its systems blocked about 91% of the attempted transfers. Its fraud-prevention system analyzes outgoing transfers in real time for signs such as giveaway scams, brand impersonation, and newly created wallet addresses, then can use an AI agent to warn customers and ask questions intended to help them recognize fraud. Coinbase said the agent had not previously encountered this specific campaign but recognized tactics including promises to multiply cryptocurrency, pressure tied to a live event, and irreversible transfers. The company said the detection and intervention process was fully automated, without human involvement.

  • The attempted transfers were authorized by legitimate account holders, which Coinbase said makes this type of fraud harder to stop than theft involving stolen credentials or compromised accounts.

Researchers at Technische Universität Berlin found that a person who physically opens some PCs can reset the TPM’s failed-PIN counter, bypassing the normal lockout protections for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs. In laboratory tests, they recovered a four-digit Windows Hello PIN on an AMD HP OmniBook 3 in 57 minutes and a six-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel Framework Laptop 13 in under seven minutes, each after 236 attempts. Based on measured speeds, they estimated that a four-digit Hello PIN could take up to 40 hours to crack rather than 69 days, while a default six-digit BitLocker PIN could take up to 20 days rather than 19 years.

The issue concerns firmware TPMs that save their state, including wrong-attempt counts, on the motherboard’s flash storage rather than in separate secure storage. On some AMD systems, researchers used a board placed between the processor and flash chip to block counter updates; on systems using certain Winbond RPMC flash chips, a brief power glitch could reveal a key used to forge counter values. AMD confirmed CVE-2026-43613 and plans firmware fixes for most affected chips between November and February 2027, while Winbond is studying its issue without a committed fix date. The researchers advise adding at least two digits to Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs, applying AMD firmware updates when available, and keeping affected devices under physical control.

  • Some AMD desktops tested without RPMC flash could have their failed-attempt count reset using an ordinary flash programmer, without the researchers’ custom interposer board.
  • Windows Hello on the tested AMD laptop still required a restart after every five wrong PIN attempts, but imposed no lockout delay once the TPM state was rolled back.

A critical Apache Roller vulnerability, CVE-2026-129448, is under active exploitation, according to the Apache Software Foundation. The issue has a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. It allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code.

The flaw is located in the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and processes vendor extension types before authenticating the requester. Apache said the issue is the same as CVE-2026-82384, which was previously patched in September 2026 with only Roller 6.1.5 listed as affected. Users should upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, or, if patching is not immediately possible, disable extension types or remove the XML-RPC servlet mapping and restart Roller.

  • Turning off XML-RPC through Apache Roller's administration interface does not protect older versions, because they process the malicious request before checking that setting.
  • The issue was previously tracked as CVE-2026-82384 with only Roller 6.1.5 listed as affected, but Apache now says it is the same flaw and that versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 are vulnerable.
  • Organizations unable to patch immediately can reduce exposure by disabling extension types in WEB-INF/web.xml or removing the XML-RPC servlet mapping, then restarting Roller.

Apache Roller, software used to run blogs, has a serious security problem that attackers are already using. The flaw lets someone take control of a Roller site’s underlying system from the internet without needing to sign in, affecting versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. People running affected sites should update to version 6.1.6 or later, because a successful attack could let outsiders run whatever commands they choose on the server.

10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers

NGINX fixed a critical, decade-old HTTP/2 flaw (CVE-2026-123007) that can let unauthenticated remote attackers execute code as an NGINX worker, with public proof-of-concept code available. Organizations should upgrade to NGINX 1.31.9 or 1.30.7 immediately, or temporarily disable HTTP/2 where upgrading is not possible.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-123007, nicknamed nginx2root, is a decade-old NGINX HTTP/2 flaw that can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code with NGINX worker-process permissions.
  • 02The flaw affects NGINX Open Source releases from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 and is fixed in versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7.
  • 03F5 also fixed four additional high-severity flaws affecting particular NGINX configurations, including HTTP/2, HTTP/3, proxy resolver, and mail-proxy setups.
  • 04Public proof-of-concept code is available, but F5, Wiz, and Rapid7 had not reported observed exploitation and CISA had not listed the flaw in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the article's publication.
  • 05Organizations that cannot immediately upgrade can temporarily disable HTTP/2 to mitigate CVE-2026-123007, but must fully restart NGINX because a configuration reload alone can leave the old executable running.

A decade-old flaw in NGINX’s HTTP/2 support, CVE-2026-123007 and dubbed “nginx2root,” can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled. The issue has been present in NGINX open-source code since version 1.9.5, released in 2015, and affects releases through 1.31.8. Code execution runs with NGINX worker-process permissions, although researchers demonstrated that it could be combined with a separate Linux SCTP flaw to obtain root access in testing. No exploitation in the wild had been reported, but public proof-of-concept code is available.

F5 released NGINX Open Source 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 to fix CVE-2026-123007 and four additional flaws that can also lead to code execution under particular configurations. The HTTP/2 flaw can be temporarily mitigated by disabling HTTP/2, but this does not address the separate HTTP/3, resolver, and mail-proxy issues. After patching, organizations need a full NGINX restart or a live binary upgrade, because a configuration reload can leave the old executable and worker processes running. CIRCL also advises watching for abnormal worker behavior, core dumps, unusual outbound activity, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy traffic but few logged requests.

  • A normal NGINX configuration reload is insufficient after patching because it can leave the vulnerable executable and existing worker processes running; a full restart or live binary upgrade is required.
  • NGINX access logs may remain clean during an attempted HTTP/2 exploit because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally appear as logged web requests.
  • Rapid7's demonstrated method required roughly 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic and depended on specific AVX-512 CPU capabilities, while slower links could exceed NGINX's default one-hour connection limit and cause the attempt to fail.
  • Disabling HTTP/2 temporarily mitigates the two HTTP/2-related flaws but does not address the separate HTTP/3, resolver, or mail-proxy flaws fixed in the same releases.
  • The reported code execution initially runs with NGINX worker-process permissions rather than full host control, although Xint demonstrated that it could be combined with a separate Linux SCTP issue to reach root access.

A long-standing flaw in NGINX, software used to run websites and online services, can let an outsider take control of part of a server simply by connecting through a commonly used web feature called HTTP/2. It affects many NGINX versions released since 2015, and public demonstration code is available, although no real-world misuse has been reported so far. Taking control would initially give an intruder the same access as the web-service program, but it could be combined with another flaw to gain full control of the host. Organizations running affected NGINX versions should install the new fixes or temporarily turn off HTTP/2.

Although no active exploitation was reported, prompt upgrading or temporary HTTP/2 mitigation is highly actionable.

Quality Isn’t The Main Worry About AI Pentesting — Data Privacy and Production Safety Are

Intruder’s survey of 500 US and UK security and engineering leaders finds that AI pentesting is being adopted rapidly to close the gap between frequent software releases and infrequent manual tests. The main adoption concerns are data privacy, safety in production, and auditable, reproducible validation—not the quality of AI testing itself.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Intruder surveyed 500 security and engineering leaders in the United States and United Kingdom about AI pentesting adoption and concerns.
  • 02Although 68% of organizations deploy production code at least daily, 47% go more than a month between full web application and API pentests, and only 4% believe their present testing frequency provides sufficient coverage.
  • 03Data privacy (40%), production-system safety (36%), and regulatory or auditor acceptance of AI pentest reports (28%) were cited as bigger adoption barriers than AI testing quality.
  • 04Fifty-five percent of organizations report using AI pentesting across their environment, while 36% have tried it without yet adopting it at scale.
  • 05Fifty-six percent of teams spend at least six hours per week validating security-tool findings, and 90% of surveyed leaders agree that a traditional annual pentest is dead.

Intruder surveyed 500 security and engineering leaders in the United States and United Kingdom on AI pentesting adoption and needs. The survey found that 68% of organizations deploy code to production at least daily, while 47% go more than a month between full tests of their web applications and APIs. Only 4% of security leaders believe their current testing frequency provides sufficient coverage, and 42% say they ship code without additional security checks between pentests.

AI pentesting is already used across the environment by 55% of respondents, while 36% have tried it without scaling adoption. The leading barriers are data privacy, safety on production systems, and whether auditors and regulators will accept AI pentest reports, rather than testing quality itself. Teams also report substantial time spent validating findings: 56% spend six or more hours a week triaging false positives, while 90% agree that the traditional annual pentest is no longer enough to keep pace with software releases.

  • The central trust problem for AI pentesting is not primarily whether it can find issues, but whether teams can see what it tested and obtain reproducible proof that a reported issue can actually be used.
  • Organizations with the fastest release cycles face a structural coverage gap: human-led full pentests cannot realistically run as often as code is deployed, leaving changes untested for weeks or months.
  • False-positive validation is a major operational cost, with more than half of teams spending at least six hours each week deciding whether security-tool findings are real.
  • Even after a fix is released, many organizations do not independently verify it in production immediately, meaning they may not know whether the weakness has actually been removed for up to two weeks.
  • Manual pentesting is increasingly expected to serve assurance and audit needs rather than remain the main method for ongoing security validation.

The article reports on a survey of 500 security and engineering leaders in the United States and United Kingdom about using AI to test software for weaknesses. Many organizations release code daily or several times a day, while thorough human-led checks often happen weeks or months apart, leaving newly introduced problems undiscovered. Companies are increasingly trying AI-based testing to check software more often, but they worry most about protecting private data, avoiding disruption to live services, and being able to prove that reported problems are real. The stakes are that software flaws can reach live systems quickly and attackers may find and use them within a day.

CISA has urged organizations to immediately patch Java4Shell, a critical Oracle Java flaw tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated 8.1 on the CVSS scale. The issue is an out-of-bounds write in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine, part of the Java Development Kit. Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM or, in certain conditions, enable unauthenticated remote code execution. Oracle and OpenJDK have released patches, and the article states there is no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

Under default settings, the flaw can reportedly allow attackers without accounts to execute arbitrary code on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker are also listed as affected where an attacker has a login. Blackpoint Cyber reported that about 28,000 unauthenticated requests with malformed Base64 authentication values caused a local Spring Boot application’s JVM to terminate after roughly 20 seconds, while additional testing showed nearby Java-object corruption and changes to live application data without an immediate crash.

CISA recommends identifying all affected Java installations, including runtimes bundled with third-party applications, container images, and appliances, and applying Java and vendor patches as soon as possible. Where patching cannot happen immediately, CISA advises restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Numerous security and software vendors have also published advisories or analyses of the flaw.

  • The practical risk differs by application: the article says attackers can run code without an account on several products under default settings, while Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker require a login.
  • Blackpoint Cyber reported that roughly 28,000 unauthenticated requests containing malformed Base64 authentication data terminated a local Spring Boot application's Java process after about 20 seconds of sustained traffic.
  • Testing cited in the article found that the flaw could corrupt nearby Java objects and alter live application data without immediately crashing the affected application.
  • Organizations may overlook affected systems because Java runtimes can be bundled inside third-party applications, container images, and appliances rather than installed separately.

The U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA is urging organizations to quickly update Oracle Java and OpenJDK after a serious flaw was found in a part of Java that handles encoded data. A specially crafted input could crash a Java-based service or, in some cases, let an outsider run their own commands on it without logging in. The issue can affect widely used business software such as Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, and Artifactory, so companies need to find all Java installations—including ones built into other software or containers—and apply available updates.

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical pre-auth Java Base64 decoder flaw that can enable memory corruption and potentially remote code execution on AVX-512 VBMI-capable x86-64 systems running affected Java 17+ builds. KEY POINTS
  • 01Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a flaw in Java’s accelerated Base64 decoder that can write 62 or 63 bytes past an output buffer before rejecting malformed input.
  • 02The vulnerable code affects Java 17.0.6 and later on supported Java 17 builds, as well as Java 21, 25, and 27, but only on x86-64 Intel or AMD processors with AVX-512 VBMI support.
  • 03Calif reported pre-authentication attacks against default deployments of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, although other labs had reproduced crashes and memory leaks rather than remote code execution.

Researchers disclosed Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, a flaw in Java’s accelerated Base64 decoder that can cause memory corruption and may allow remote code execution. Calif said attacks can work without a login against default deployments of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Other researchers reproduced crashes, memory leaks, and local memory reads, but had not reproduced remote code execution.

The issue affects Java 17.0.6 and later Java 17 builds, plus Java 21, 25, and 27, only on x86-64 Intel and AMD processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI. A malformed Base64 string ending in an extra equals sign can write 62 or 63 bytes beyond its intended output before Java rejects it. Oracle, OpenJDK, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, and SAP released fixes, while Red Hat was still preparing updates; organizations that cannot update can temporarily disable the affected Base64 speed-up feature with a JVM option.

  • Whether a deployment is exposed can vary between servers running the same container image, because the vulnerable decoder runs only on x86-64 processors with four required CPU features, including AVX-512 VBMI.
  • The malformed Base64 input is rejected only after it writes beyond its intended memory area, meaning error handling does not prevent the memory corruption.
  • A proxy that waits for complete requests, such as nginx in its default configuration, can block some reported attack paths but does not protect against all of them.
  • The article says a Java program that merely opens a TLS connection to a malicious server may also be at risk, even if it does not provide a network service itself.
  • Failed exploitation attempts can crash the Java process, and public tests showed repeated malformed login requests could cause a Spring Boot application to crash.

Researchers disclosed Java4Shell, a flaw in certain newer Java versions that may let someone send specially malformed data to crash a server or, in some cases, take control of it without having an account. It can affect services including Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, Confluence, and Artifactory when they run on certain newer Intel or AMD server chips. This matters because Java is widely used in business software, so vulnerable organizations could face outages or unauthorized access until they install updated Java versions or apply a temporary setting that disables the unsafe speed-up feature.

This is a critical, newly disclosed Java flaw with potential pre-authentication remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise applications including Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, and Confluence.   • 04Affected products include BIG-IP modules, BIG-IP APM, BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP DNS, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes, and, for certain flaws, BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition (CNF).

F5 disclosed six critical vulnerabilities in BIG-IP that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM), interrupting traffic until the service restarts. F5 says the flaws may also enable remote code execution, though none of its advisories reports active exploitation. All six are rated 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP’s traffic-processing data plane.

The issues require specific virtual-server configurations, including particular iRule commands or an APM per-request policy containing Client Information and Endpoint Security agents. Affected offerings include BIG-IP modules, BIG-IP APM, PEM, DNS, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes, and, for certain flaws, BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition. F5 has released engineering hotfixes as the only fix for the critical issues and provides no workaround until those hotfixes are installed.

  • Exposure to the six critical flaws is configuration-dependent: each requires a particular traffic rule or access-policy setup on a virtual server, rather than affecting every BIG-IP deployment by default.

  • Organizations running unsupported BIG-IP versions cannot assume they are unaffected, because F5 only evaluated releases that remain within technical support.
  • F5's advisory and the CVE record disagree on whether BIG-IP CNF is affected by CVE-2026-120722, with the advisory listing CNF as not vulnerable while the updated CVE record lists it as affected.
  • One additional lower-rated iControl SOAP flaw can permit a network-connected user with only the Guest role to issue unauthorized management requests that may run system commands, modify files, or disable services.

F5 disclosed six serious flaws in its BIG-IP traffic-management products that could let an outsider crash the part of a system that handles most network traffic, interrupting access until it restarts. The problems affect organizations using BIG-IP with certain customized traffic rules or access-policy settings, as well as some cloud-native versions of the product. F5 says the flaws might also allow someone to take control of affected systems, and there is no general temporary fix, so customers need vendor-provided emergency updates.

Attackers Compromise Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI Package to Steal Cloud Credentials

Malicious releases 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft’s agent-framework PyPI package installed Python startup hooks that stole cloud credentials and CI/CD tokens, then exfiltrated them to a webhook.site endpoint. Users who installed the versions should isolate affected systems, rebuild from clean environments, and rotate exposed credentials.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers published malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft’s agent-framework package on PyPI on November 17, 2026, and both releases were later quarantined.
  • 02The malicious package versions placed files in Python’s installed-package directory that caused credential-stealing code to run whenever Python started, including when pip ran.
  • 03The code collected selected environment variables, credential files, Azure DevOps OIDC tokens, Azure managed-identity tokens, and Azure virtual-machine metadata.
  • 04The stolen data was compressed, encoded, and sent by HTTPS to a hard-coded webhook.site address.
  • 05Users who installed the malicious releases are advised to isolate affected hosts, use the safe 1.26.0 version from a clean environment, investigate exposure, and rotate credentials from a clean system.

Attackers compromised Microsoft’s agent-framework package on PyPI and published malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on November 17, 2026, 33 minutes apart. The releases were designed to steal credentials, cloud identity tokens, and environment information, then send the data to a hard-coded webhook.site endpoint. Both versions have been quarantined, although it is unclear how the attackers obtained publishing access. Agent-framework is Microsoft’s open-source Python framework for building and orchestrating AI agents and receives roughly 190,000 downloads per month.

The malicious package wheels installed .pth files in the Python site-packages directory, causing the stealer to execute whenever Python starts, including when pip runs, without the package being explicitly imported. The code targeted Azure CLI files, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, Git credentials, Docker configuration, Hugging Face files, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, Azure managed-identity tokens, and Azure instance metadata. Affected users are advised to isolate impacted hosts and runners, pin agent-framework to safe version 1.26.0 from a clean environment, search logs for requests to the identified webhook.site address, rotate exposed credentials from a clean system, and audit Azure identities and GitHub Actions workflows that deploy to Azure.

  • The malicious code could execute on every Python launch without anyone importing Agent Framework, because it used Python startup configuration files placed in the installed-package directory.
  • The stealer did not only read credentials already stored on disk; it could ask Azure services to issue new identity tokens, so rotating existing saved secrets alone may not address all exposure.
  • Version 1.26.2 expanded collection to GitHub Actions identity tokens and additional credential-related environment variables, increasing risk for automated deployment workflows.
  • Network and DNS logs can be checked for connections to the hard-coded webhook.site address, providing a concrete way to identify possible data theft.

Attackers uploaded two harmful versions of Microsoft’s Agent Framework software package to PyPI, a popular place where programmers download Python tools. Anyone who installed those versions may have had cloud logins, stored passwords, and access tokens from services such as Azure, Azure DevOps, and GitHub Actions collected and sent to the attackers. The harmful code could run whenever Python started, even if the affected package was not actively being used. This shows that compromising a widely used software package can put many developers’ computers and automated software-building systems at risk.

CISA added CVE-2026-115731, a critical Perforce Puppet flaw with a CVSS score of 9.4, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reports of active exploitation. The issue affects Puppet’s report-processing code and can allow a client with a certificate signed by the certificate authority to execute arbitrary code on a Puppet Server under the service account. If certificate requests are automatically approved without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker may be able to obtain a valid certificate and use the flaw.

Affected software includes specified Puppet Enterprise, Puppet Core, and OpenVox releases, and fixes are available from Perforce and OpenVox. Researcher Alain Rödel of Neodyme AG also reported CVE-2026-115732, a critical certificate-name authorization bypass affecting Puppet and OpenVox. Neodyme said that control of a Puppet Server could enable theft of certificate-authority signing keys and impersonation of other hosts, while Puppet’s central access to corporate systems could make ransomware deployment, mass data theft, and movement across a network possible.

  • A Puppet certificate authority that automatically approves requests without strong checks can allow an unauthenticated network attacker to obtain the certificate needed to exploit CVE-2026-115731.
  • Successful code execution on a Puppet Server could allow an attacker to steal the certificate-authority signing keys and impersonate other managed hosts.
  • The reported impact depends on the Puppet Server configuration and whether orchestration protocols are enabled, but code execution on the server remains serious in any configuration.
  • A Reddit user reported tracing an intrusion involving CVE-2026-115731 after finding a severely misconfigured certificate authority shortly after the vulnerability’s public disclosure.

U.S. cyber officials say criminals are actively using a serious flaw in Puppet, software that organizations use to manage large numbers of computers from a central server. The flaw can let someone with an approved digital credential, or someone who can obtain one from a poorly configured system, run their own commands on that central server. Affected organizations using certain Puppet Enterprise, Puppet Core, or OpenVox versions should install the available updates, because control of a Puppet server could let attackers spread ransomware, steal data, or move through the wider company network.

Bitdefender reported that the suspected Chinese APT behind EggStreme has substantially rebuilt its malware toolkit while continuing to target Philippine government organizations. The revised framework uses a different network protocol, an expanded command set, campaign-specific certificate authorities, and a passive version that waits for an operator to connect rather than contacting an external command-and-control server. EggStreme still uses DLL sideloading and can profile systems, establish persistence, run payloads in memory, conduct reconnaissance, move through networks, and transfer files. Suspected China-linked spying groups are targeting government organizations in the Philippines and elsewhere in Southeast Asia with updated software designed to secretly take control of computers and steal information. Other campaigns used fake diplomatic meeting documents and compromised outdated Microsoft email servers to install similar remote-control tools. OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Critical Memory Corruption ( CVE-2026-114938 )

CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a high-severity OpenJDK Base64 decoder memory-corruption flaw that can potentially enable unauthenticated remote code execution on susceptible x86-64 systems with AVX-512 VBMI. Organizations should promptly patch affected JDK 17, 21, 25, and 27 deployments or temporarily disable Base64 intrinsics/AVX-512 if patching is delayed.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-114938, also called Java4Shell, is a heap-based buffer overflow in OpenJDK’s optimized Base64 decoder that can corrupt JVM memory when specially crafted input ending in padding characters is processed.
  • 02The issue affects compatible x86-64 systems with AVX-512 VBMI support and is not reported to affect ARM64 systems, standard Java 8, Java 11, or Java 17.0.0 through 17.0.5.
  • 03Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026, and Oracle assigned the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 with network access, no privileges, and no user interaction required.
  • 04Researchers demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate.
  • 05If patching is delayed, the article recommends temporarily disabling Base64 hardware acceleration with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or disabling AVX-512 on x86-64 systems with -XX:UseAVX=2.

CVE-2026-114938, nicknamed Java4Shell, is a critical memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK’s optimized Base64 decoder. On compatible x86-64 systems with AVX-512 VBMI support, attacker-controlled Base64 input can cause the decoder to write beyond its allocated memory before Java rejects malformed input. Oracle assigned the issue a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and described exploitation as difficult, while Calif Research assigned a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. Researchers demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate.

The issue affects OpenJDK release lines 17, 21, 25, and 27, including several distributions built from OpenJDK, while ARM64, standard Java 8, Java 11, and Java 17.0.0 through 17.0.5 are not affected according to the article. Successful exploitation depends on the Java version, processor capabilities, and whether an application passes untrusted Base64 data to the vulnerable decoder. Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026, and organizations are advised to update affected Java runtimes, including bundled runtimes in containers and appliances. If patching is delayed, the article recommends temporarily disabling Base64 hardware acceleration with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or disabling AVX-512 on x86-64 with -XX:UseAVX=2.

  • Malformed Base64 input may still corrupt memory before Java rejects it, because the vulnerable decoder can write a full 64-byte block beyond its allocated output buffer.
  • External exposure scanning may not be sufficient to determine risk because both the precise Java runtime and the host processor’s capabilities may not be visible externally.
  • Having the required Linux CPU flags—avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2—does not by itself establish that an application is exploitable; the application must also decode untrusted Base64 data through an affected JDK.
  • A public proof of concept reproduces the memory corruption, but the article reports no known exploitation in the wild and no CISA KEV listing as of November 18, 2026.

A serious flaw called Java4Shell was found in some newer versions of Java, a widely used software platform, that can let specially crafted data damage a running application’s memory. It affects certain 64-bit Intel- and AMD-style computers with a particular advanced processor feature, and researchers showed that it could be used before login against default installations of products such as Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate. If successfully abused, an outsider could potentially read sensitive information, disrupt an application, or take control of the affected Java process, so organizations should install the vendor fixes promptly.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a high-severity patch advisory for a potential remote code execution path in widely used OpenJDK-based Java deployments, with demonstrations against several common enterprise products. Although exploitation is described as difficult and no in-the-wild abuse is reported, affected organizations need to identify susceptible runtimes and apply vendor fixes promptly.

Google Picked Your Agency, Unless the Badge Link Says Gooqle

A phishing campaign impersonated Google Partners with a convincing Premier Partner Badge invitation that passed SPF, DKIM, and Microsoft composite authentication, but its button led to the newly registered lookalike domain gooqlepartnership[.]com. The case shows that valid email authentication verifies the sending domain, not the legitimacy of the destination or request.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A phishing email impersonating Google Partners offered a UK IT-services employee a Google Premier Partner Badge invitation and used the recipient’s full name and Google-style branding.
  • 02The message passed SPF, DKIM, and Microsoft composite authentication, while Microsoft assigned it a spam confidence level of 5 and placed it in the Junk folder.
  • 03The Accept Invitation button used a mail-platform click tracker to redirect recipients to gooqlepartnership[.]com, a lookalike domain replacing the “l” in Google with “q.”
  • 04The lookalike domain was registered nine days before the email was delivered, was fronted by Cloudflare, and had redacted registrant information.
  • 05IRONSCALES quarantined two campaign messages sent to mailboxes in the same tenant under different subject lines, and a human analyst classified the incident as malicious.

A digital marketing employee at a UK IT-services company received a phishing email titled “Google Premier Partner Badge Invitation” that impersonated Google Partners. It used the recipient’s full name, Google-style branding, a Google copyright footer, and praise for strong Google Ads performance. A second mailbox in the same tenant received a variant titled “Your Google Premier Partner Badge Is Available,” and IRONSCALES quarantined both messages before a human analyst classified the incident as malicious.

The message passed SPF, DKIM, and Microsoft composite authentication, but Microsoft assigned it a spam confidence level of 5 and delivered it to Junk rather than blocking it. Its Accept Invitation button passed through a mail-platform click tracker and redirected to gooqlepartnership[.]com, a lookalike domain that substitutes a q for the l in Google. The domain was registered nine days before delivery, was fronted by Cloudflare, and had a redacted registrant; the article notes that the landing page was not observed, so it does not claim a credential form or download was present.

  • Email authentication checks can confirm that a sending domain authorized a message without establishing that the message’s brand claim or linked destination is legitimate.
  • A reward-based lure, such as recognition for strong Google Ads performance, can bypass training focused on spotting urgent or threatening requests because it gives the recipient a reason to feel proud rather than alarmed.
  • The decisive evidence in this case was the button’s final destination, where a one-letter domain substitution turned “Google” into “Gooqle,” rather than any failed authentication result.
  • Subject-line-based detection alone would have been incomplete because the same campaign used two different subjects within one organization.
  • The article does not establish what the destination site would have done, because the landing page was not observed and the available screenshot only showed a generic 404 response.

A fake email told employees at a UK IT-services company that their agency had earned a Google advertising badge, using Google-like branding and the recipient’s full name to make the message feel genuine. Clicking its “Accept Invitation” button would have sent them to a newly created website whose name looked like Google but replaced one letter. The email passed common checks meant to confirm that it came from the domain that sent it, showing that those checks cannot prove a message or link is trustworthy. This matters to organizations because flattering, believable messages can trick staff into visiting harmful sites even when email filters and technical checks do not flag them.

This is a concrete phishing campaign analysis showing how a Google-themed lookalike domain bypassed SPF, DKIM, and composite authentication. It is useful for email-security professionals, but the observed campaign was limited to two mailboxes and the final payload was not observed.

Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, was publicly disclosed on November 17, 2026 as a critical memory-corruption issue in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. The article states that the vulnerable code originated in an AVX-512 performance optimization merged into OpenJDK in June 2021. It affects only x86-64 CPUs that support AVX-512 VBMI; ARM systems are not affected. Oracle’s listed fixed releases are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1.

Aikido reconstructed the original OpenJDK pull request and ran its Deep Review product against it, reporting three high-severity findings. One finding identified the Java4Shell issue: malformed Base64 input with invalid padding could trigger an integer underflow, produce an incorrect output mask, and cause a 64-byte write beyond the allocated destination buffer. The tool recommended falling back to a safer decoder when fewer than four input bytes remain, which the article says is essentially the same as the eventual upstream fix. Deep Review also identified an oversized vectorized write and an incomplete invalid-character check, both of which were subsequently corrected upstream.

  • A single extra “=” after 128 otherwise valid Base64 characters could cause the AVX-512 decoder to calculate a negative value and then write a full 64-byte block where it should write nothing.
  • Deep Review reported two additional defects in the same original implementation: a 64-byte write into space intended for 48 decoded bytes and an invalid-character check that omitted one of four input lanes.
  • The article states that the recommended mitigation was to send inputs with fewer than four remaining bytes to a safer decoding path, matching the upstream fix except for an equivalent instruction comparison.
  • Aikido says its Deep Review system was isolated from the internet while analyzing the recreated pull request, so it did not rely on the later public fix to produce its findings.

The article says that a serious flaw in Java’s built-in Base64 text-decoding feature was added in 2021 and publicly revealed in 2026. On affected x86-64 computers with a particular newer processor feature, specially malformed input could make a program write outside its intended memory area, potentially letting an attacker take control. The issue does not affect ARM systems, and organizations using affected Java versions should update to the fixed releases. It also argues that reviewing code changes before they are released can catch dangerous mistakes years before they become widely known security problems.

AuditTeam used its OpsAgent framework to compromise dozens of organizations across at least seven countries between January and October 2026. The group presents its extortion as an “Audit & Consulting fee,” promising a vulnerability report in exchange for payment while threatening to publish stolen data. Observed victims were in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong, and Russia, while its leak site claimed additional victims in other countries.

OpsAgent provides remote control capabilities including file and process management, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture, shellcode injection, and movement between compromised systems. Specialized modules can disable security products using a digitally signed Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus driver, terminate database and backup services, encrypt files, remove shadow copies, and leave a ransom note. The framework evolved from C++ to Rust, used Amazon CloudFront subdomains for command-and-control communications, and could retrieve its server address through a public GitHub repository.

A group called AuditTeam has broken into dozens of organizations in multiple countries, then demanded payment while pretending the money is for a security review. Its software can steal information, watch users, shut down security protections, move through an organization’s computers, and lock files so they cannot be used. Organizations in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong, and Russia were observed as victims, and the group claims victims in several other countries. This matters because the group has built increasingly capable tools and uses widely shared internet services to make its communications harder to block without affecting legitimate users.

Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a heap overflow in Java’s hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. Researchers at Calif reported that it can enable unauthenticated code execution in applications including Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, Confluence, Artifactory, and PingFederate under default settings. Oracle and the OpenJDK project released fixes on November 17, 2026, while CISA urged organizations to patch immediately. As of November 18, 2026, the article reports no known exploitation in the wild.

A system is exposed only if it uses an affected Java build, runs on an x86-64 processor supporting AVX-512 VBMI, and processes attacker-controlled malformed Base64 through Java’s standard decoder. The affected fast-processing routine can write 62 or 63 bytes past an output buffer when Base64 data ends with an unexpected equals sign, before Java rejects the malformed input. Independent testing reproduced crashes and memory reads, while Calif demonstrated code execution, although reliable exploitation requires target-specific work. Organizations should install fixed Java releases and restart affected services; if patching is delayed, they can disable the vulnerable Base64 optimization with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics JVM option.

  • Java rejects the malformed Base64 input only after the decoder has already written past the allocated memory, so validation performed inside an application cannot prevent the underlying write.
  • Products that include their own Java runtime require an update from the product vendor; updating only the system-wide Java installation may leave them exposed.
  • A failed exploitation attempt commonly crashes the Java process, meaning even unsuccessful attempts can cause service outages and can often be retried.
  • The article warns that using -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock alone prevents Java from starting, while -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics is the recommended temporary workaround.

Java4Shell is a newly disclosed flaw in some newer versions of Java that can let specially crafted text cause a Java program to crash and, in certain applications, potentially let an outsider take control without signing in. It affects only servers using particular Intel or AMD processors, so identical software may be at risk on one machine but not another. Organizations running services such as Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, Confluence, or Artifactory should install updated Java software or temporarily turn off the faulty fast-processing feature, because easy-to-trigger crashes can disrupt services and researchers have demonstrated that takeover is possible.

  • 04Organizations should update to vendor-fixed Java releases, restart all JVMs and rebuild container images, or temporarily disable the accelerated path with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.
  • 05As of November 18, 2026, the article states that no exploitation in the wild had been confirmed.

OpenJDK and Oracle released fixes on November 17, 2026, for CVE-2026-114938, also called Java4Shell, a heap overflow in HotSpot’s accelerated Base64 decoder. The issue affects certain Java 17, 21, 25, and 27 builds on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI and related instruction features. A specially malformed Base64 value can cause the decoder to write beyond the end of a Java memory buffer before Java rejects the input. Oracle rates the issue CVSS 3.1 8.1 (High).

The vulnerable code is a hand-written assembly optimization used after the JVM’s C2 compiler makes Base64 decoding a frequently used path. It mishandles the final padded Base64 characters and can overwrite up to 62 bytes beyond the intended buffer in Calif’s reproducer. The basic and URL-safe Base64 decoders are affected, while the MIME decoder uses a different path. ARM64 systems, x86-64 systems without AVX-512 VBMI, OpenJDK 8 and 11, and Java 17.0.0 through 17.0.5 are not affected.

The immediate consequence can be an unauthenticated JVM crash, while Calif reports that application-specific memory manipulation can potentially lead to information disclosure and remote code execution. The researchers reported pre-authentication remote code execution in default installations of several products, including Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, but product-specific exploit chains remain undisclosed. Organizations should update all Java runtimes, including bundled and containerized copies, restart running JVMs, and rebuild container images. Where patching is delayed, the article recommends disabling Base64 intrinsics with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.

  • A malformed Base64 value can trigger the out-of-bounds write even though Java subsequently throws an IllegalArgumentException, meaning application logs may show a normal-looking decode error after memory has already been corrupted.
  • The vulnerable decoder path is used only after the JVM has processed enough valid Base64 data for its compiler to optimize the method, so a one-off request to a newly started service may not reproduce the issue.
  • Hardware is a decisive exposure condition: ARM64 hosts and x86-64 systems lacking AVX-512 VBMI do not run the vulnerable routine, even if they use an otherwise affected Java version.
  • Disabling only the Base64 optimization with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics is a narrower temporary mitigation than disabling AVX-512 with -XX:UseAVX=2.
  • Updating a Java installation alone is insufficient if services continue running old JVM processes or use older Java runtimes embedded in third-party products or container images.

OpenJDK and Oracle fixed a flaw called Java4Shell that can let specially crafted Base64 text overwrite nearby data in a Java program’s memory. It affects certain newer Java versions running on compatible Intel or AMD computers, including Java software and packaged products that accept untrusted data such as login information or web requests. The likely result is a program crash, but researchers say it can sometimes be turned into a way for an unauthenticated outsider to take control of affected services, so organizations should update their Java installations promptly.

Microsoft agent-framework on PyPI: .pth hook steals Azure and CI credentials

Malicious PyPI releases agent-framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 used Python .pth startup hooks to silently steal environment secrets, cloud credentials, and Azure/GitHub Actions OIDC tokens from affected systems. Remove the hooks before running pip, reinstall version 1.26.0, and rotate potentially exposed credentials.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft’s agent-framework package were published to PyPI on November 17, 2026, and have since been removed.
  • 02Both releases used a .pth startup file that caused their credential-collection code to run during normal Python startup without an application explicitly importing the package.
  • 03The code collected secret-related environment variables, credential files, data from other processes, and Azure managed-identity tokens, while version 1.26.2 also requested GitHub Actions OIDC tokens.
  • 04Collected data was compressed, encoded, and sent through HTTPS to a webhook[.]site URL.
  • 05Affected users should remove the malicious .pth hooks before running pip, reinstall and pin agent-framework version 1.26.0, and rotate potentially exposed secrets.

Malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft’s agent-framework package were published to PyPI on November 17, 2026, before being removed. Both releases added code that automatically ran during normal Python startup, even if an application did not import the package. The code collected credentials and other sensitive information and sent it to a webhook[.]site URL. Version 1.26.0 does not contain the malicious code.

The releases used .pth files in site-packages to trigger the collector whenever Python starts normally. The collector gathered secret-related environment variables, credentials from files and other processes, and Azure managed-identity tokens; version 1.26.2 additionally requested GitHub Actions OIDC tokens. Affected environments may include system Python installations, virtual environments, Conda environments, containers, and CI caches. The article advises removing the malicious .pth hooks before running pip, reinstalling and pinning agent-framework==1.26.0, blocking the known upload destination, rotating exposed secrets, and reviewing Microsoft Entra ID activity for unusual token use.

  • Version 1.26.2 placed its collector in a new top-level module, leaving the agent_framework_meta package byte-identical to version 1.26.0, so a comparison limited to that package would miss the malicious change.
  • The malicious code can run when tools such as pip start Python, so the article advises deleting the .pth startup hooks before using pip to remove the package.
  • The collector sets the _AF_TEL environment variable so it generally runs once per process tree, then continues to execute again when a new Python process tree starts while the package remains installed.
  • Rotating stored passwords and keys alone may not address the exposure, because the code also requested temporary Azure managed-identity and CI/CD identity tokens that require review of Microsoft Entra ID activity logs.

Two harmful versions of Microsoft’s agent-framework software were briefly posted to the Python package download service PyPI. Once installed, they could automatically collect passwords, access tokens, cloud account information, and other sensitive data from computers and automated build systems, then send it to an outside website. People and organizations that installed versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 may need to remove them and replace exposed credentials, because stolen access could be used to reach cloud services and software-development accounts.
