The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains

Threat actors are using immutable public blockchains—including Bitcoin, EVM smart contracts, TRON, and Solana memo transactions—as resilient dead drops for encrypted C2 configuration data that cannot be conventionally taken down. Defenders should shift from domain blocklists toward detecting anomalous blockchain JSON-RPC queries and in-memory decryption activity on endpoints.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Threat actors are using public blockchains as resilient dead drop resolvers to store encrypted command-and-control configuration data that cannot be removed through conventional domain or hosting takedowns.
  • 02The Glupteba botnet used Bitcoin transactions to retrieve AES-encrypted command-and-control domains and fallback addresses from public Electrum server queries.
  • 03EtherHiding uses EVM-compatible smart contracts to store encoded command-and-control destinations that malware can retrieve through read-only JSON-RPC calls such as eth_call.
  • 04Researchers reported that North Korea-aligned actors, including UNC5342 and UAT-12643, have used blockchain-based mechanisms involving BNB Smart Chain, TRON, or Solana memo transactions to obtain payload locations or command-and-control URLs.
  • 05The article recommends that defenders monitor anomalous outbound blockchain JSON-RPC activity, inspect unexpected encoded data in requests, and detect in-memory decryption before malware contacts the resolved destination.

Threat actors are increasingly using public blockchains as durable repositories for command-and-control (C2) configuration data, replacing centralized servers and domains that defenders can seize, sinkhole, or block. Encrypted C2 addresses, payload locations, and instructions can be stored in immutable transaction records, smart contracts, wallet activity, or Solana memo data. This removes the traditional single point of failure associated with a hardcoded C2 domain or IP address. Malware can retrieve the data through public blockchain services and then connect to the current operational destination.

The article describes earlier Bitcoin-based use by the Glupteba botnet, which queried Electrum servers and extracted AES-encrypted C2 information from transactions. It also describes EtherHiding, in which actors use EVM-compatible smart contracts, including BNB Smart Chain contracts, to store encoded C2 destinations retrieved through read-only eth_call requests. UNC5142, linked to ClearFake, and North Korea-linked UNC5342 are cited as groups that adopted this technique, while UAT-12643 is described as using Solana Memo Program transactions to store encrypted C2 URLs. TRON is also presented as part of multi-chain fallback designs that can make disruption more difficult.

The article argues that traditional domain blocklists and hosting takedowns are insufficient when the C2 discovery information is preserved across decentralized ledgers. It recommends baselining legitimate blockchain use and detecting automated or high-frequency outbound JSON-RPC calls, including eth_call, getTransaction, and getSignaturesForAddress. Defenders are also encouraged to inspect suspicious encoded data in RPC traffic and prioritize endpoint telemetry that can identify in-memory decryption before malware connects to a resolved C2 server.

  • Read-only smart-contract queries such as eth_call let malware retrieve current command-and-control details without creating a new blockchain transaction, so the retrieval itself leaves no transaction record on the ledger.
  • Although blockchain records are immutable, smart contracts can hold configuration values that attackers update through later transactions, allowing compromised systems to obtain replacement destinations without receiving a new malware binary.
  • Solana memo transactions can provide a lightweight update channel: an attacker can publish a new encrypted destination in a fresh transaction, and malware can retrieve the newest transaction associated with a wallet during its next polling cycle.
  • The article notes that blocking a single malicious website or server is insufficient when attackers use multiple chains such as BNB Smart Chain, TRON, and Solana as fallback sources for command-and-control information.
  • The same public blockchain lookups used by malware can resemble legitimate activity, making behavioral monitoring of automated JSON-RPC calls and endpoint memory more useful than static domain blocklists alone.

The article explains how criminal and state-backed groups can hide the internet addresses used to control harmful software inside public blockchain records, which are shared widely and cannot easily be removed. Infected computers can look up these hidden addresses and receive new instructions even after defenders shut down known websites or servers. This affects organizations and individuals whose devices are compromised, and it makes stopping long-running malicious campaigns harder because defenders must watch for suspicious connections to blockchain services instead of only blocking bad websites.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a broad trend and best-practice analysis rather than reporting a single new incident or urgent defensive action. It is useful for professionals who monitor C2 infrastructure because it consolidates concrete examples of blockchain-based dead drops and relevant detection approaches.

CVE-2026-114938 is an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1. An attacker who successfully exploits it can run arbitrary code within the Java process using the permissions of the account that runs the service. A public proof of concept is available, although the article states that no in-the-wild exploitation was confirmed and the issue was not in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at the time of writing.

Exposure requires both an affected Java release and an x86-64 host with the avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2 processor flags; ARM hosts, including AWS Graviton, are not affected. Affected environments can include internet-facing Java application servers and platforms such as Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, Jira, Confluence, and Keycloak, especially where Java is bundled in installers or container images. Oracle fixed the issue in its 17 November 2026 Critical Patch Update, and until patching is confirmed, the article recommends verifying the actual runtime used by each service, disabling BASE64 intrinsics as an interim measure, restricting public access to Java administration and build interfaces, and monitoring for unexpected child processes.

  • The same container image can be vulnerable on one cloud instance type and not on another because exposure depends on the host processor’s instruction-set features.
  • Most assets in the reported exposure set were identified from their service fingerprints rather than confirmed Java version checks, so they should be treated as potentially affected until both the runtime version and processor features are verified.
  • Organizations may miss affected systems because Java is often bundled within application installers or container images and may not be tracked as a separate asset.
  • Updating a host’s system Java may not fix an affected application if that application uses its own bundled Java runtime.
  • The exposure was spread across multiple industries rather than concentrated in one sector, indicating that the Java runtime itself is the central risk factor described in the article.

The article warns about a serious flaw in certain versions of Oracle Java and related Java software that could let an outsider take control of a running Java application without logging in. It affects internet-facing services only when they use one of the listed Java versions on certain Intel- or AMD-style computers with specific processor features; standard Java 8 and 11 and ARM-based systems are not affected. This matters because Java runs many widely used business services, including build tools, software repositories, customer portals, and identity systems, and the Java version is often hidden inside bundled software or containers. Organizations should install the available updates, check the Java software each service actually uses, and limit public access until fixes are confirmed.

Researcher Jerry Gamblin found that 3,901 of MITRE’s 4,509 CVEs published in the 52 weeks ending November 16, 2026, carried a datePublished value of exactly 00:00:00.000Z. MITRE said its older workflow requires a client-supplied time value and uses midnight for stability because of concurrency issues in the legacy architecture.   • The inaccurate timestamps can make MITRE appear substantially slower to publish records than other organizations, even though records from other CVE publishers showed a comparable median change-log delay of 4.5 minutes.

MITRE said an older system gave thousands of its public vulnerability entries a publication time of midnight even though they were actually posted later that day. This affects researchers and automated tools that use those times to judge how quickly security information becomes available and to compare organizations that publish vulnerability records. MITRE plans to stop using the older system in early 2027, but past records may keep their inaccurate times, making it harder to reconstruct when important security information was publicly available.

Censys confirmed affected sites through sinkhole referrers and found that an Optimizely script on Zoom loaded track.js from 1688360[.]cc. Optimizely said an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation product to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and said it fixed the issue, removed the injected code, and secured affected accounts.

The track.js payload collected payment-card details, replaced copied cryptocurrency addresses with attacker-controlled wallets, and sent page URLs, cookies, and browser-rendered page images to collection endpoints. It delivered further iOS stages to iPhone, iPad, and touch-screen Mac visitors, while non-iOS visitors received the skimmer, clipper, and page-data collection code without the exploit chain. Censys linked the infrastructure to MCH control panels, a Caishen iOS exploit backend, and cryptocurrency energy-rental storefronts, but noted that the shared channel code was a hard-coded kit default and did not identify a specific operator.

The campaign’s two staging hosts and implant command-and-control host went offline on November 17, shortly after disclosure, while five new MCH panel hosts appeared within about a day. Blockchain records showed cryptocurrency payments arriving on November 16, with some Tron and Ethereum proceeds moving through commercial services within hours. Censys assessed that the operator likely rented the loader and used existing tooling rather than developing bespoke infrastructure.

  • The MCH panel and Caishen backend were broadly deployed across unrelated hosts and registrants, indicating that title matches alone are insufficient to attribute a specific deployment to this campaign.

Malicious code was inserted into outside services used by major websites, causing visitors to sites including BBC, Zoom, CNN, DoorDash, Zillow, Fox News, and GitLab to receive it without realizing it. On computers, it could steal payment-card details, replace copied cryptocurrency payment addresses with the criminals’ addresses, and collect page information; on some Apple phones and tablets, it tried to load further harmful software. The incident shows that even trusted websites can put visitors at risk when a service they rely on is compromised, and the operators were able to move stolen cryptocurrency quickly and rebuild parts of their operation after it was exposed.

StepSecurity has made its Secure Registry available at no cost through a community tier for public GitHub repositories using GitHub-hosted runners and the Harden-Runner GitHub Action. The service is integrated with Harden-Runner, which can automatically configure supported JavaScript package managers to use the StepSecurity Community Secure Registry. Its default protections delay newly published package versions for two days and block versions known to be compromised. Harden-Runner Insights records package requests and shows whether they were allowed, held by the cooldown, or blocked.

Users can enable the service by placing Harden-Runner first in a job and setting secure-registry: true; existing commands such as npm ci remain unchanged. The first release supports npm, pnpm, and Bun, and the community registry is hosted at community.registry.stepsecurity.io/javascript/. The article’s example workflow allowed is-number@7.0.0, blocked a recent TypeScript development version because it was within the two-day cooldown, and blocked chalk@5.6.1 as a known compromised package. Cached dependencies are not checked, and packages using another preconfigured npm registry are left unchanged and are not evaluated by Secure Registry.

  • If a repository already uses a different npm registry, Harden-Runner leaves that configuration unchanged, meaning those package downloads are not evaluated by Secure Registry.
  • Cooldown exemptions can allow newly published packages sooner, but they cannot override blocks for versions known to be compromised.
  • For public repositories, Secure Registry package-request insights are public, matching the visibility of GitHub workflow logs.

StepSecurity has made its Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use GitHub-hosted runners, connecting it to its Harden-Runner tool. It checks JavaScript software packages before they are downloaded during automated project builds, delaying very new versions for two days and refusing versions known to be harmful. This matters because a bad update from a widely used package can enter many projects automatically, while the new service gives developers a way to reduce that risk and see which downloads were allowed or stopped.

Microsoft agent-framework PyPI Package Compromised

Microsoft's PyPI agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were compromised with a Python .pth startup-hook credential stealer that runs on every Python launch, harvests secrets, mints CI/CD and cloud identity tokens, and exfiltrates them to webhook.site. Organizations that installed either version should remove it, pin to 1.26.0, investigate webhook.site egress, and treat all credentials and federated trust available on affected hosts or CI runners as compromised.
KEY POINTS
  • 01PyPI quarantined Microsoft agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 after they were found to contain credential-stealing code, while version 1.26.0 is identified as the last clean release.
  • 02The malicious packages used a Python startup configuration file that caused the payload to run whenever Python started, without requiring users to import agent-framework.
  • 03The payload collected environment variables, credential files, and secrets from other running processes, then sent collected data to a webhook.site endpoint.
  • 04Version 1.26.2 added the ability to request fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions and also targeted Azure DevOps and Azure managed identity token services.
  • 05The article advises organizations that installed either affected version to remove the package, pin to version 1.26.0, rotate secrets, review cloud trust relationships, and search network logs for webhook.site connections.

Microsoft’s agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were uploaded to PyPI on November 17, 2026 with credential-stealing code and were later quarantined. Version 1.26.2 was uploaded after version 1.26.1 had already been quarantined, indicating that the publishing access used for the releases remained available. The article identifies version 1.26.0, released November 12, as the last clean release. The affected releases were distributed as wheels only and used RestSharp rather than PyPI trusted publishing.

The malicious code was installed as a Python .pth startup hook, causing it to execute whenever Python starts without requiring an import of the affected framework. It collected host details, sensitive environment variables, credential files, and secrets from other running processes, then sent the data to a specified webhook.site endpoint. It also requested fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure managed identity services, increasing the potential impact beyond stolen static credentials. The article advises affected organizations to remove the malicious versions, pin to 1.26.0, rotate exposed secrets, review federated cloud trust relationships, and search network logs for connections to webhook.site.

  • The attacker uploaded version 1.26.2 only 2 minutes and 23 seconds after PyPI quarantined version 1.26.1, showing that the publishing access used for the malicious releases remained available after the first response.
  • Because the payload was installed as a Python startup hook, it could run during any later Python command, such as testing or build tooling, even when agent-framework was never imported.
  • The payload detached its collection process from the program that launched Python, so it could continue sending data without appearing in CI job output and may outlive the job that triggered it.
  • The malware could request new short-lived identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure managed identity services, meaning changing previously exposed passwords or keys alone does not remove all risk.
  • The malicious wheels closely copied the legitimate package metadata and changed only the version string, while being uploaded as wheels without source distributions, making ordinary package-page review less likely to reveal the tampering.

Two infected versions of Microsoft’s agent-framework package were briefly uploaded to PyPI, a website developers use to download Python software. Anyone who installed them could have had passwords, cloud access details, and other private information copied and sent to an attacker whenever they later started Python, even if they never used the package itself. This especially affects developers and companies using automated build systems, because the malicious code could also create fresh temporary login credentials for services such as GitHub, Azure DevOps, and Microsoft Azure. Removing the package is not enough: affected users must change exposed passwords and access keys and review who or what can access their cloud accounts.

How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)

Cloudflare released managed WAF rules to detect Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical OpenJDK Base64-decoding flaw that can enable remote code execution on affected AVX-512-capable x86-64 systems. The WAF rules provide temporary defense-in-depth, but organizations must update all Java runtimes and restart affected services to fully remediate the issue.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder that can enable heap-memory disclosure and remote code execution.
  • 02The issue affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later on x86-64 systems with AVX-512 VBMI support when an application decodes attacker-controlled Base64 data; ARM64 systems are not affected.
  • 03Cloudflare added managed WAF rules for paid plans to detect malformed Base64 patterns associated with Java4Shell, but enables them in Log mode by default because legitimate traffic can resemble exploit attempts.
  • 04Updating every affected Java runtime and restarting its services is the complete remediation, while disabling Base64 intrinsics or AVX-512 can provide a temporary mitigation.
  • 05Cloudflare states that its WAF cannot cover all attack paths, including non-HTTP traffic, internal traffic that bypasses Cloudflare, encoded data, and malicious outbound connections.

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder, disclosed by Calif on November 17, 2026. It affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer when attacker-controlled Base64 data is decoded on supported x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI; ARM64 systems are not affected. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against several products in default configurations, including Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate.

The flaw occurs in the optimized Base64 code used on certain processors, where malformed padding can produce a negative output length and cause a 64-byte write beyond the allocated output array. Java later rejects the input and throws an exception, but the adjacent memory has already been overwritten. OpenJDK and Oracle released patched builds on the day of disclosure, and organizations must update every Java runtime—including bundled and containerized copies—and restart affected services.

Cloudflare released managed WAF rules to detect Java4Shell-related malformed Base64 input for paid plans, with the rules enabled in Log mode by default because legitimate traffic can resemble exploitation attempts. Customers can review matching requests and change the rules to Block, while Business and Enterprise customers can also use WAF Attack Score for additional detection of exploit-chain payloads. Cloudflare emphasizes that the WAF is only a defense-in-depth measure because it cannot cover paths such as non-HTTP traffic, internal traffic, encoded data, or malicious outbound connections.

  • The malformed input is eventually rejected by Java, but the memory overwrite occurs before the error is raised, so application-level validation cannot prevent the corruption.
  • A simple trigger can be 64 "A" characters followed by "="; on OpenJDK 17, the article says the fast decoding path requires 128 characters followed by "=" instead.
  • The managed WAF rules are set to Log rather than Block by default because benign application-specific token formats can resemble the malformed Base64 patterns.
  • Updating a system-wide Java package may not fix applications that bundle their own Java runtime or use container images, and each updated service must be restarted.
  • Cloudflare says its machine-learning RCE scoring may be more useful for accompanying exploit stages and later command traffic than for the initial malformed Base64 trigger alone.

A newly disclosed flaw called Java4Shell affects many versions of Java, a widely used software foundation, and could let an outsider send specially malformed data to take control of vulnerable applications. It can affect Java services running on certain newer Intel and AMD server processors, including products such as Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and Elasticsearch when they process attacker-provided encoded data. Cloudflare has added optional web traffic checks to help spot these attempts, but the real fix is for organizations to update every affected Java installation and restart the services using it. The issue matters because Java is used across many business systems, and web filtering cannot protect systems reached through internal connections, non-web traffic, or malicious outbound connections.

Threat Hunting On The Network: An Active Search for Risks on the Wire

Network threat hunting proactively identifies malicious behavior by analyzing flow records, proxy and VPN logs, and packet captures for anomalies that static perimeter signatures may miss. Start with available tools and a focused protocol, using behavioral baselines to investigate unusual internal and external traffic.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Network threat hunting actively searches packet data for malicious activity, while endpoint threat hunting relies more heavily on logs.
  • 02Firewalls and intrusion detection or prevention systems can miss threats because adversaries evolve faster than static signatures and vendor or threat-intelligence updates.
  • 03Behavioral analysis uses network baselines to identify unexpected protocols and traffic flows rather than relying only on byte sequences, file hashes, and documented exploits.
  • 04Useful network-hunting data sources include flow records, proxy logs, VPN logs, and full packet captures.
  • 05Hunters should examine internal traffic as well as external traffic for unusual activity, such as unexpected SSH access or large overnight downloads.

Network threat hunting is the active search for malicious activity in network packet data, as distinct from endpoint hunting, which relies more heavily on logs. It is intended to find risks that firewalls and intrusion detection or prevention systems may miss when adversaries change techniques faster than static signatures and intelligence updates can keep pace. Rather than examining every packet manually, hunters can use network information to identify suspicious patterns.

Behavioral analysis compares activity with normal network baselines to detect unexpected protocols, traffic flows, and access patterns. Relevant data sources include NetFlow or IPFIX records, HTTP/HTTPS proxy logs, VPN appliance logs, and full packet captures, while tools named include SIEM platforms, Elasticsearch and Kibana, Zeek with RITA, Arkime, and Wireshark or TShark. Useful indicators include unusual port use, DNS anomalies, failed authentication attempts, certificate or TLS anomalies, and unusual internal activity such as unexpected SSH access or large overnight downloads.

  • A network hunter does not need to manually inspect every captured packet; flow records, indexed packet tools, and focused searches can narrow the investigation.
  • Behavioral hunting can remain effective even when threat actors change their tools and procedures because their activity still produces fundamental network behaviors.
  • Internal traffic can be as important to investigate as inbound traffic, since unusual employee access patterns or large off-hours transfers may reveal risk.
  • Beginning with one protocol and tools already available is presented as a practical way for less-experienced analysts to start threat hunting.

The article explains how security teams can actively look through network activity for signs of harmful behavior instead of relying only on automated defenses to block known threats. Organizations are affected because criminals can change their methods faster than security tools are updated. By learning what normal activity looks like, teams can spot unusual actions, such as unexpected remote connections or very large downloads at odd hours, before they become a serious incident.

This is evergreen educational guidance on network threat hunting, behavioral analysis, data sources, and tools rather than a report of a specific incident or urgent finding. It is useful for practitioners building hunting skills but does not require immediate attention.

Why Cloud Behavioral Baselining Matters for AI-Driven Offensive Attacks

AI-driven offensive frameworks such as ARTEX accelerate reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and cloud control-plane abuse, but their changing code and infrastructure make static signatures unreliable. Defenders should baseline identity and cloud API behavior to detect anomalous, rapid attack sequences regardless of the tool used.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that threat actors used the AI-driven ARTEX framework in live intrusions, including one sequence that generated 27 events in 23 seconds.
  • 02ARTEX connects a language model to established security tools and lets agents plan, execute, observe results, and adapt their next actions toward an objective.
  • 03Framework-specific signatures are fragile because attackers can fork ARTEX, swap models, rewrite prompts, rotate infrastructure, or mix multiple frameworks.
  • 04The article recommends baselining cloud identity and control-plane activity, including normal API calls, role assumptions, source locations, account relationships, and changes to sensitive services.
  • 05The article advises turning confirmed behavioral patterns, such as rapid discovery-to-data-access sequences and unusual API volume from non-human identities, into repeatable detections.

Google Threat Intelligence Group reported on October 30, 2026, that threat actors were using the ARTEX agentic offensive framework in live intrusions. ARTEX connects a language model to established security tools and allows agents to plan actions, execute them, review results, and adapt when an attempt fails. GTIG observed one ARTEX sequence produce 27 events in 23 seconds, and documented cases in which attackers moved from an initially compromised account to deep system access in as little as 15 minutes.

The article argues that identifying a specific framework is not a durable detection strategy because attackers can fork code, change models and prompts, rotate infrastructure, or combine frameworks. Instead, organizations should establish normal patterns for cloud identities and control-plane activity, including API usage, role assumptions, source locations, resource access, and changes to sensitive settings. Examples of suspicious behavior include a narrowly used service identity suddenly making large volumes of listing calls, rapid role-assumption chains, unusual permission checks using AWS DryRun flags, and discovery-to-data-access sequences occurring seconds apart.

  • Agentic offensive frameworks can recover from failed steps: GTIG documented a case in which an ARTEX-deployed webshell failed and the framework appeared to refactor its approach and try again.
  • ARTEX activity included using AWS DryRun flags and placeholder IDs to test compromised IAM permissions against EC2, EBS volumes, and snapshots before taking actions.
  • Non-human identities are especially useful for behavioral baselining because their normal activity is narrower and more predictable than human activity.
  • The same cloud API calls may be normal for one identity but suspicious for another, so detections need to combine identity context with network and resource context.
  • GTIG assessed that current agentic frameworks trade stealth for speed, creating detectable bursts in which reconnaissance, exploitation, and privilege changes can occur seconds apart.

The article describes ARTEX and similar AI-powered tools that can help attackers quickly test systems, adapt when a step fails, and move through online cloud accounts with little human guidance. Google’s threat researchers reported seeing ARTEX used in real break-ins, where one rapid sequence created 27 recorded actions in 23 seconds. Organizations that use cloud services are affected because stolen accounts can be used to search for data, gain more access, and change important settings. Since attackers can easily rename or alter these tools, the article argues that organizations should watch for unusual account behavior rather than rely only on known tool names or internet addresses.

automated systems concept

Automation concept

control panels concept
Control panels are management screens attackers or administrators use to configure systems and view activity.
Control plane concept
A control plane is the part of a system that manages configuration, decisions, and coordination rather than carrying user data.
Conventional Fuzzing technique
Conventional fuzzing is automated security testing that sends many unusual inputs to software to find crashes or flaws.
cookies concept
Cookies are small pieces of data websites store in a browser to remember logins, settings, or tracking information.
cooldown concept
A cooldown is a waiting period before something can happen again.
Coordinated Monitoring concept
Coordinated monitoring means organizations working together to watch for problems, threats, or disruptions.
Coordinated or State-Sponsored Attack concept
An attack planned by multiple parties or carried out with support from a government.
Corelight organization
Corelight is a cybersecurity company that provides network detection and response products.
Corporate Applications concept
Software and online services used by employees to do work for their organization.
Corporate data concept
Corporate data is information owned or used by a company, such as files, emails, customer records, and business plans.
corporate network concept
A corporate network is the private collection of computers, servers, and systems used by an organization.
corporate networks concept
Corporate networks are the connected computers, servers, and systems used by a company.
also: internal corporate systems
corporate VPN services product
Company-run virtual private network services that let employees securely connect to internal systems over the internet.
Coruna malware
Coruna is a named malware family, cyber tool, or threat label referenced in security reporting.
Counterfeit concept
A counterfeit item is a fake product made to look like a genuine one.
Court of Arbitration for Sport organization
The Court of Arbitration for Sport is an international body that resolves legal disputes involving sports.
CPU concept
A CPU is the main processor in a computer that runs instructions and performs calculations.
CPUs concept
Central processing units, the main chips that perform a computer's instructions.
CreateRemoteThread technique
CreateRemoteThread is a Windows function that attackers can abuse to make another process run injected code.
credential concept
A credential is proof of identity for logging in, such as a password, security token, API key, or certificate.
credential collection technique
The process of harvesting usernames, passwords, and tokens, typically by malware or phishing, to gain unauthorized access.
credential files concept
Credential files are files that store login secrets such as passwords, API keys, tokens, or certificates.
credential form concept
A credential form is a login-style form that asks users to enter information such as usernames, passwords, or codes.
credential rotation technique
Credential rotation means replacing passwords, keys, or tokens with new ones to reduce the risk from stolen or old credentials.
credential stealer malware
A credential stealer is malware designed to steal usernames, passwords, tokens, or other login information.
also: credential-collection code, stealer payload
credential stealing code malware
Credential stealing code is software designed to steal usernames, passwords, tokens, or other login secrets.
credential theft technique
Credential theft is the stealing of usernames, passwords, tokens, or other login information.
credential-phishing
Credential phishing is a scam that tricks people into entering usernames, passwords, or codes into a fake login page.
credentials concept
Credentials are login details or access tokens that prove a user or system is allowed to access something.
credit unions organization
Credit unions are member-owned financial institutions that offer banking services.
critical infrastructure concept
Critical infrastructure refers to essential systems and services that societies and organizations depend on.
critical infrastructure operators organization
Critical infrastructure operators are organizations that run essential services such as power, water, transport, or communications.
Critical Infrastructure Resilience concept
The ability of essential services, such as power or healthcare, to withstand and recover from disruptions including cyberattacks.
critical issues concept
Critical issues are problems considered urgent because they can cause major harm, such as system compromise or serious service disruption.
Critical Patch Update concept
Oracle’s Critical Patch Update is a regular bundle of security fixes for Oracle products.
critical remote code execution vulnerability
Critical remote code execution is a severe security flaw that lets an attacker run code on a system from afar.
Critical services concept
Critical services are essential systems or functions whose failure would seriously harm operations or public services.
Critical Software concept
Software that is important enough that failures or compromise could seriously affect an organization or service.
critical vulnerabilities vulnerability
Critical vulnerabilities are very serious security flaws that could let attackers cause major damage or gain major access.
crypto-address clipping technique
Crypto-address clipping is malware behavior that replaces a copied cryptocurrency wallet address with an attacker's address.
cryptocurrency concept
Cryptocurrency is digital money, such as Bitcoin, that uses cryptography and usually runs on a blockchain.
also: virtual currency
cryptocurrency accounts concept
Cryptocurrency accounts are wallets or exchange accounts used to hold, send, or receive digital assets.
Cryptocurrency Accounts and Wallets concept
Accounts and software or devices used to hold and manage cryptocurrency funds.
also: victims' cryptocurrency accounts and wallets
cryptocurrency address concept
A cryptocurrency address is a public identifier used to send and receive funds on a blockchain.
Cryptocurrency Addresses concept
Public identifiers used to send and receive funds on a cryptocurrency network.
cryptocurrency clipper malware
A cryptocurrency clipper is malware that swaps copied wallet addresses so payments go to the attacker instead of the intended recipient.
Cryptocurrency Giveaway technique
A cryptocurrency giveaway is often a scam that promises to return more crypto to people who send money first.
cryptocurrency payments concept
Cryptocurrency payments are transfers of digital currency such as Bitcoin or Ethereum instead of traditional money.
Cryptocurrency seed phrases concept
Cryptocurrency seed phrases are secret recovery words that can give full access to a crypto wallet.
also: seed phrases
Cryptocurrency Transfers concept
Cryptocurrency transfers are movements of digital money such as Bitcoin or Ethereum between online wallets.
cryptocurrency wallet product
A cryptocurrency wallet is software or hardware used to store and use the keys that control digital coins.
cryptocurrency wallet address replacement technique
A theft technique that changes a copied cryptocurrency wallet address to an attacker's address before a payment is sent.
cryptocurrency wallet addresses concept
Cryptocurrency wallet addresses are strings of letters and numbers used as destinations for sending digital currency.
also: Ethereum-style, Tron and Bitcoin replacement addresses
cryptocurrency-address-replacement technique
Cryptocurrency address replacement is a technique that swaps a victim's wallet address for an attacker's address before a payment is sent.
Cryptography concept
Cryptography is the use of mathematical methods to protect information from being read or changed by unauthorized people.
Cryptor tool
A cryptor is software used to disguise malware so antivirus tools have a harder time detecting it.
Cryptor Module malware
A ransomware component that encrypts victims' files and may disrupt recovery options.
CSRF technique
CSRF is a web attack where a site is tricked into performing an action using a logged-in user's session without the user's intent.
also: CSRF tokens
CSV concept
CSV can mean comma-separated values, a simple spreadsheet-like file format, or cluster shared volumes in Windows clustering depending on context.
CSV Exports concept
CSV exports are data files that store rows of information in a simple comma-separated format.
cursor
Cursor is an AI-assisted code editor built for software developers.
Customer accounts concept
Customer accounts are user records and logins that let customers access a company's services.
customer data concept
Customer data is information a company keeps about its customers, such as names, contact details, or purchase history.
customer information concept
Customer information is data a business keeps about its customers, such as names, contact details, purchases, or account records.
customer portals concept
Customer portals are websites where customers log in to view information, get support, or manage services.
Customer Projects concept
Individual websites, applications, or hosting environments managed for separate customers.
CVE vulnerability
A CVE is a public identifier used to track a specific known software vulnerability.
CVE Numbering Authorities organization
CVE Numbering Authorities are approved organizations that assign CVE identifiers to publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
also: CNAs, CNA
CVE Program organization
The CVE Program is the global system that assigns standard identifiers to publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
CVE record concept
A CVE record is the public entry that describes and tracks a specific known cybersecurity vulnerability.
CVE records concept
CVE records are public entries that identify and describe known cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
CVEs concept
CVEs are standardized public identifiers for known cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
CVSS concept
CVSS is a standard scoring system used to rate how severe a software vulnerability is.
also: CVSS score: 9.8
CVSS 3.1 concept
CVSS 3.1 is version 3.1 of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System used to rate the severity of security flaws.
also: CVSS 3.1 base score
CVSS 4.0 concept
CVSS 4.0 is a standard scoring system used to rate how serious a software vulnerability is.
CVSS scale concept
The CVSS scale is a standard 0-to-10 scoring system used to describe how severe a security vulnerability is.
CVSS score concept
A CVSS score is a standard number used to show how severe a software vulnerability is.
also: CVSS score: 8.1
CVSS score of 9.8 concept
A very high rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, indicating a critical security flaw.
CVSS v3.1 concept
CVSS v3.1 is a standard scoring system used to describe how serious a software vulnerability is.
CVSS v3.1 Score concept
A standardized numerical rating used to show how severe a software vulnerability is likely to be.
CWE-122 vulnerability
A Common Weakness Enumeration category for software bugs that write too much data into memory allocated on the heap.
cyber concept
Cyber is a broad shorthand for things related to computers, networks, and digital security.
Cyber Crisis Management concept
Cyber crisis management is the organized response to a serious cyber incident that disrupts an organization.
Cyber Crisis Plans concept
Cyber crisis plans are prepared instructions for how an organization should respond to a serious cyber incident.
also: response plans
Cyber defense concept
Cyber defense is the work of protecting computers, networks, and data from digital attacks.
cyber incident concept
A cyber incident is any event where digital systems, accounts, or data may have been attacked, exposed, or disrupted.
cyber incidents concept
Cyber incidents are events that threaten or harm computer systems, networks, or data.
cyber operations concept
Activities conducted in cyberspace including espionage, sabotage, or defense, typically by state-sponsored groups.
Cyber Risk Level concept
A cyber risk level is an assessment of how likely or serious cyber threats are at a given time.
cyber strategy concept
A plan for preventing, responding to, and reducing cyber threats.
cyber threats concept
Cyber threats are possible dangers to computers, networks, or data caused by attackers or malicious software.
cyberattack concept
A cyberattack is an attempt to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems or data.
cybercrime concept
Cybercrime is crime carried out using computers, networks, or the internet.
cyberespionage technique
The use of computer networks to conduct espionage, usually by state-sponsored groups to steal secrets from governments or corporations.
Cybersecurity concept
Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, software, and data from digital attacks or misuse.
cybersecurity companies organization
Cybersecurity companies are businesses that sell services or products to help protect computers, networks, and data.
Cybersecurity Systems concept
Cybersecurity systems are tools and services used to protect computers, networks, and data from attacks.
cybersecurity-and-infrastructure-security-agency organization
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is the U.S. government agency that helps defend critical infrastructure and improve cybersecurity.
CyberStrikeAI tool
An open-source framework referenced in security reporting that uses a language model to help direct actions on compromised systems.
CyCognito organization
CyCognito is a cybersecurity company known for external attack surface management technology.
Daily Cyber Headlines product
A recurring news resource that summarizes cybersecurity headlines.
DarkSword malware
DarkSword is a named malware family, threat, or cyber tool referenced in security reporting.
Data access concept
Data access means the ability to view, use, change, or retrieve information from a system.
data breach concept
A data breach is an incident where sensitive, private, or protected information is accessed, exposed, or stolen without permission.
data centers concept
Data centers are facilities full of servers and networking equipment that run websites, cloud services, and business systems.
Data collection concept
Data collection is the process of gathering information from people, systems, devices, or services for analysis or use.
data exposure concept
Data exposure means sensitive information is left accessible to people or systems that should not be able to see it.
data governance concept
The rules, responsibilities, and processes an organization uses to manage data safely, accurately, and legally.
Data Handling concept
Data handling is the way information is collected, stored, used, shared, and protected.
data leak concept
A data leak is when private or sensitive information is exposed to people who should not have it.
Data Plane concept
The data plane is the part of a system that handles actual user data, as opposed to the management functions that configure the system.
data privacy concept
The right and practice of protecting personal and sensitive information from unauthorized access, collection, or exposure.
Data Quality concept
A measure of whether data is accurate, complete, current, and useful.
Data Sources concept
Data sources are systems, services, or devices from which information is collected.
data theft concept
Data theft is the stealing of information from a system or service.
data was stolen concept
Data was stolen means information was copied or taken by someone who was not authorized to have it.
Dataset concept
A dataset is an organized collection of information used for analysis, reporting, or training software.
DbgInjector technique
A process-injection technique that abuses debugging features and hardware breakpoints to run shellcode in another process.
DbgInjector technique
A process-injection technique that abuses debugging features and hardware breakpoints to run shellcode in another process.
dead drop resolver technique
A dead drop resolver is a technique malware uses to find its command server by retrieving hidden instructions from public online locations.
also: dead drops
Dead-drop resolvers technique
Dead-drop resolvers are hidden online locations or services that malware checks to find instructions or the address of its control server.
Debian product
A well-known community-driven Linux distribution famous for its stability and package management system.
deception technique
Deception is tricking a person or system into believing something false, often to gain access or hide activity.
decoder tool
A decoder is software or code that converts encoded or compressed data back into a readable or usable form.
decryption concept
Decryption is the process of turning scrambled encrypted data back into readable information.
Deep Review tool
Deep Review is Aikido's automated code-review tool for finding security and quality problems in software changes.
deepfake concept
A deepfake is fake audio, video, or imagery made with AI to make someone appear to say or do something they did not.
deepfakes concept
Realistic but fake images, videos, or audio created using artificial intelligence to show someone saying or doing something they never did.
defaced technique
Defaced means a website has been altered without permission, often to show an attacker’s message.
defacement technique
Defacement is when an attacker changes a website or screen to show unauthorized content.
Default configurations concept
Default configurations are factory or out-of-the-box settings that may be unsafe if not changed.
defenders concept
Defenders are the people or teams responsible for protecting systems and responding to cyber threats.
Defense Contractors organization
Defense contractors are companies that supply products or services to military or government defense organizations.
defense evasion technique
Defense evasion means techniques attackers use to avoid being detected or blocked by security tools.
Defense in depth concept
Defense in depth is a security strategy that uses multiple layers of protection so one failure does not expose everything.
Defrost Settings concept
Controls that determine when and how refrigeration equipment removes frost buildup.
Deidentification technique
Deidentification is the process of removing or altering personal details so data is less likely to identify someone.
Deidentified concept
Deidentified describes data that has had obvious personal details removed or altered to reduce identification risk.
deleted concept
Deleted means removed from normal access, though copies may sometimes still exist in backups, logs, or recovery areas.
denial-of-service
Denial-of-service is an attack that overwhelms a system so legitimate users cannot access it.
also: DoS
Department of Homeland Security organization
The Department of Homeland Security is a U.S. government department responsible for domestic security, including cyber defense.
dependencies concept
Dependencies are outside software components or libraries that an application needs in order to work.
dependency concept
A dependency is outside software that an application relies on, which can create risk if that outside component is vulnerable or malicious.
Deployments concept
The process of releasing software, configuration changes, or services into a live environment.
deserialization flaw vulnerability
A deserialization flaw is a software bug where unsafe data is loaded back into a program in a way attackers can abuse.
deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability
Deserialization of untrusted data is a dangerous software flaw where an app reads attacker-controlled data as objects, potentially letting the attacker run code or change behavior.
also: deserializes
Destination Buffer concept
A destination buffer is a reserved area of computer memory where software writes output data.
Detect technique
Detect means to identify suspicious or malicious activity in systems, networks, or data.
detection concept
Detection is the process of finding signs of suspicious or malicious activity.
Detection Coverage concept
The extent to which security tools can identify known threats, behaviors, or weaknesses.
detection guidance concept
Detection guidance is advice that helps defenders find signs of suspicious or malicious activity in their systems.
detections concept
Alerts or findings generated by security tools indicating that a potential threat or malicious activity has been identified.
detector tool
A detector is a security rule, model, or tool that looks for signs of suspicious or malicious activity.
Dev Machine Guard tool
Dev Machine Guard is a security tool or product name referenced in reporting.
Developer credentials concept
Developer credentials are usernames, passwords, keys, or tokens that let someone access software development systems such as code repositories or build servers.
Developer machines concept
Developer machines are computers used by software developers to write, build, and test code.
development teams organization
Development teams are groups of people who build and maintain software or products.
DHS organization
DHS is the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, a federal agency responsible for public safety, border security, and cybersecurity missions.
Digest protocol
An HTTP authentication method that avoids sending a password directly by using a cryptographic challenge response.
Digital Operational Resilience Act concept
The Digital Operational Resilience Act is a European Union regulation requiring financial organizations to manage and test their cyber and technology resilience.
digital services concept
Digital services are online or computer-based services such as websites, apps, portals, and cloud systems.
digitally signed concept
Digitally signed means software or data includes a cryptographic stamp meant to prove who created it and whether it was changed.
Digitally Signed Driver concept
A hardware driver whose publisher's identity and file integrity are verified with a digital signature.
also: valid digital signature
Director of National Intelligence organization
The Director of National Intelligence is the U.S. official who oversees and coordinates the country’s intelligence agencies.
Disclosure concept
Disclosure is the act of reporting or publishing information about a security issue so it can be understood and fixed.
discord product
Discord is a communication platform for text, voice, and video chats, popular with gaming and online communities.
also: Discord servers
Discord webhook tool
A Discord webhook is a special URL that lets software automatically send messages or files to a Discord channel.
Discord webhooks tool
Discord webhooks are special URLs that let software automatically send messages or data to Discord channels.
Discovery technique
Discovery is the attacker activity of learning about a victim’s systems, accounts, and network before taking further action.
disruption concept
Disruption is an interruption that prevents systems, services, or operations from working normally.
distinct() technique
A data-processing operation that removes duplicate entries from a dataset.
DKIM protocol
DKIM is an email signing method that helps verify that a message was authorized by a domain and was not changed after signing.
also: DKIM signature
DLL sideloading technique
DLL sideloading is an attack where malware places a fake DLL where a trusted Windows program will load it.
DLL Sideloading technique
A technique where a trusted program is tricked into loading a malicious library file instead of the real one.
DMARC protocol
DMARC is an email policy check that uses SPF or DKIM alignment to help determine whether a message claiming to come from a domain should be trusted.
DNS protocol
DNS is the internet system that turns human-readable names like example.com into the numeric addresses computers use to find websites and services.
DNS Resolution protocol
The process of translating a website or service name into the numerical network address needed to reach it.
DNS resolver concept
A DNS resolver is the service that looks up human-readable website names and finds the internet addresses computers use to connect to them.
DNS tunneling technique
DNS tunneling is a technique that hides data inside DNS requests and responses to bypass normal network controls.
docker
Docker is a platform for packaging and running applications in containers.
Docker container product
A Docker container is a lightweight, isolated environment for running an application and its dependencies.
domain controllers product
Domain controllers are servers that manage logins, permissions, and security policies in a Windows domain.
Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) technique
Algorithms that generate many changing internet domain names so malware can find its controllers.
also: DGAs, DGA, domain generation algorithms
DoorDash organization
DoorDash is a food delivery and logistics company.
DORA concept
DORA is the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, a regulation requiring financial organizations to manage technology and cyber risks.
download-and-execute technique
Download-and-execute is a malware behavior where a program retrieves another file from the internet and runs it on the victim’s device.
DryRun Flags technique
Options that let a command test or preview an action without actually making the change.
Duo product
Duo is a security product that provides multi-factor authentication and access protection.
Earth Alux threat-actor
Earth Alux is a named threat-actor group referenced in security reporting.
EBS Volumes product
Amazon Web Services virtual disk drives that provide persistent storage for cloud computers.
EC2 product
Amazon EC2 is Amazon Web Services’ cloud service for renting virtual servers.
Eclipse Temurin product
A widely used community-built distribution of OpenJDK.
EDR killer tool
An EDR killer is a tool or malware component designed to disable endpoint security software.
EggStreme malware
EggStreme is a malware toolkit made up of multiple components that attackers use to compromise and control systems.
EggStremeAgent malware
EggStremeAgent is a backdoor malware component that lets attackers collect information, move through systems, and steal data.
EggStremeLoader malware
EggStremeLoader is a malware loader that starts other components of the EggStreme toolkit.
egress concept
Egress is outbound traffic or data leaving a network, system, or cloud environment.
Egress Logs concept
Records of data and network traffic leaving a computer system or network.
Elasticsearch product
A search and analytics engine widely used to index, search, and analyze large volumes of data, often part of the Elastic Stack.
electrum product
A popular software wallet used to store, send, and receive Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.
Electrum Servers product
Public servers used by Electrum cryptocurrency wallet software to obtain Bitcoin network information.
email access concept
Email access means the ability to read, send, or manage someone’s email account, which attackers often want because it can unlock other services.
email addresses concept
Email addresses are the unique names people use to send and receive email, such as user@example.com.
email authentication concept
Technical methods that verify an email came from the domain it claims and hasn't been forged.
email filters tool
Email filters are rules or tools that sort, block, or flag messages based on their content, sender, or reputation.
Email security concept
Email security protects inboxes and users from threats such as phishing, malware, and scam messages.
Emergency Updates concept
Emergency updates are software fixes released quickly to address serious bugs or security problems.
Employee communications concept
Employee communications are messages and other information exchanged by an organization's staff.
Employee credentials concept
Employee credentials are usernames, passwords, tokens, or other login details used by workers.
employee data concept
Employee data is information an organization keeps about its workers, such as names, contact details, job records, or payroll information.
Employee Directories concept
Lists containing employee names, roles, contact details, and sometimes organizational information.
employers organization
Employers are people or organizations that hire workers and may hold sensitive employee information.
enabledForExtensions concept
A configuration option that controls whether a feature is enabled for extensions.
Encrypt technique
Encrypt is the process of turning readable data into scrambled data that only someone with the right key can read.
Encrypt files technique
To scramble files so they cannot be read without the correct decryption key.
encrypted concept
Encrypted data has been scrambled so that only someone with the right key can read it.
encrypted messaging app product
An encrypted messaging app protects messages so they are harder for outsiders to read while they are being sent.
encryption concept
Encryption is a way of scrambling information so only someone with the right key can read it.
also: encrypt systems, encrypted systems, encrypted files
endpoint concept
An endpoint is a user device such as a laptop, phone, or server that connects to a network.
endpoint security concept
Endpoint security is protection for user devices such as laptops, desktops, and phones.
endpoint telemetry concept
Endpoint telemetry is activity data collected from computers, servers, or mobile devices to help detect and investigate security issues.
endpoints concept
Endpoints are user-facing devices such as laptops, desktops, or phones that connect to systems and data.
Engineering hotfixes concept
Urgent, targeted software fixes provided by a vendor before or outside normal update releases.
engineering leaders concept
Engineering leaders are managers or senior staff responsible for guiding software or technical teams.
enterprise applications product
Enterprise applications are software systems used by organizations to run business functions such as HR, finance, sales, or operations.
Entra ID product
Microsoft's cloud identity and access-management service for users, applications, and organizations.
entry points concept
Entry points are the places where attackers can first get into a system or network.
environment variable concept
An environment variable is a setting stored by an operating system or application that programs can read while they run.
also: process-environment filter
environment variables concept
Environment variables are named settings stored by an operating system or runtime that programs can read while they run.
also: credential-related environment variables
EPSS concept
EPSS is a scoring system that estimates how likely a software vulnerability is to be exploited in the real world.
Equinor organization
Equinor is a Norwegian energy company that produces oil, gas, and renewable energy.
espionage concept
Espionage is spying to gather information without permission.
Espionage Campaign concept
An espionage campaign is a coordinated spying operation intended to gather secret or sensitive information.
Essential Services concept
Services people depend on for daily life and public safety, such as power, water, healthcare, and government services.
eth_call protocol
eth_call is an Ethereum JSON-RPC method used to simulate a smart contract call without actually changing the blockchain.
ethereum
Ethereum is a blockchain platform used for cryptocurrency, smart contracts, and decentralized applications.
also: Ethereum-style
Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) protocol
The shared computing environment that runs smart contracts on Ethereum-compatible blockchains.
also: Ethereum Virtual Machine, EVM-compatible
EtherHiding technique
EtherHiding is a technique where attackers hide malicious code or instructions in blockchain smart contracts.
europe
Europe is a continent often referenced in cybersecurity reporting involving regulations, victims, threat activity, or law enforcement.
European authorities organization
European authorities refers to government or law-enforcement agencies in Europe involved in investigations or enforcement actions.
european-union
The European Union is a political and economic union of European countries that also creates cybersecurity and privacy rules.
evade detection technique
To evade detection means to hide malicious activity so security tools or analysts do not notice it.
event logs concept
Event logs are records created by computers and applications that show important actions, errors, and security activity.
EVM protocol
EVM, or Ethereum Virtual Machine, is the runtime environment that executes smart contracts on Ethereum-compatible blockchains.
executable concept
An executable is a file that can run as a program on a computer.
Execute arbitrary code technique
To execute arbitrary code means an attacker can make a system run commands or software of their choosing.
Execute code concept
Execute code means to make a computer run instructions, which is dangerous if an attacker can run their own code.
Execution technique
Execution is the stage where an attacker runs code or commands on a target system.
exfiltrated technique
Exfiltrated means data was secretly copied or moved out of a system by an attacker.
Exfiltrates technique
Exfiltrates means secretly takes data out of a system or network without permission.
exploit technique
An exploit is code or a method that takes advantage of a security flaw to make something happen that should not be allowed.
exploit attempts technique
Exploit attempts are tries to use a software weakness to break into or disrupt a system.
exploit chain technique
A sequence of multiple security exploits used one after another to break into a system step by step.
exploit kit tool
An exploit kit is a package of tools criminals use to automatically find and exploit vulnerable browsers, plugins, or systems.
exploitation technique
Exploitation is taking advantage of a weakness in software or people to gain unauthorized access or control.
exploitation attempts technique
Exploitation attempts are tries to take advantage of a software weakness to gain access, run code, or cause harm.
Exploitation in the wild concept
Exploitation in the wild means attackers are actively using a vulnerability against real targets, not just testing it in a lab.
Exploited technique
Exploited means attackers successfully took advantage of a weakness in software or a system.
Exploited List concept
An exploited list is a list of known security vulnerabilities that have been observed being used in real attacks.
Exploits technique
Exploits are code or techniques that take advantage of software vulnerabilities.
Export concept
Export means sending goods, software, technology, or services from one country to another.
Exposed concept
Accessible in a way that could allow a threat to reach or affect a system.
exposed credentials concept
Login details that have been accidentally published or stolen, granting unauthorized access.
Exposed Data concept
Information that may have been viewed, copied, or made accessible to people who were not supposed to have it.
exposed secrets concept
Exposed secrets are leaked passwords, API keys, tokens, or other sensitive credentials that attackers could use.
Exposed services concept
Network-connected systems or applications that are reachable by people or devices outside the organization.
Extort concept
To extort someone means to pressure or threaten them into paying money or doing something.
extortion concept
Extortion is pressuring someone to give up money, data, or something valuable through threats.
extortion campaign technique
An extortion campaign is a series of threats or attacks meant to force victims to pay money or take action.
f5
F5 is a company that provides application delivery, load balancing, web security, and NGINX products.
also: vendor
failed authentication attempts concept
Failed authentication attempts are unsuccessful tries to log in or prove identity to a system.
Fake videos concept
Fake videos are videos that have been fabricated or altered to mislead viewers.
fallback concept
A fallback is a backup option used when the preferred option is unavailable or fails.
false positive concept
An alert that mistakenly flags benign activity as malicious, causing unnecessary work and potentially distracting from real threats.
false positives concept
False positives are alerts that incorrectly label harmless activity as suspicious or malicious.
fbi organization
The FBI is the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation, which investigates cybercrime and national security threats.
federal agencies organization
Federal agencies are government organizations that operate at the national level.
Federal Aviation Administration organization
The U.S. government agency that regulates civil aviation and air-travel safety.
Federal Bureau of Investigation organization
The Federal Bureau of Investigation is the main U.S. federal law-enforcement agency that investigates crimes including cybercrime.
Federal Civilian Executive Branch organization
Federal Civilian Executive Branch refers to U.S. federal civilian agencies that are part of the executive branch.
also: FCEB
Federal Lawmakers organization
Federal lawmakers are elected national-government officials who create and vote on laws.
Federated identity credential concept
A federated identity credential is a cloud trust setting that lets an external identity, such as a workflow, sign in without storing a long-term password.
also: federated identity credentials, federated credential configurations, federated credentials
Federation concept
Federation is a setup where separate services or servers agree to communicate and share identity or content without being one central system.
file encryption concept
File encryption scrambles files so they cannot be read without the right key or password.
File hashes concept

SMS phishing messages technique

social engineering technique

social engineering attacks technique
Social engineering attacks are tricks that manipulate people into revealing information or doing something unsafe.
software development concept

software engineers concept
Software engineers are people who design, build, test, and maintain software.

Software flaws are mistakes or weaknesses in programs that can cause bugs or create security risks.

Software repositories are locations where source code and related project files are stored and managed.
software supply chain concept

software updates concept

software vulnerability vulnerability

Optional notes attached to Solana blockchain transactions that can store small pieces of text or data.

Source Distributions concept

south-korea

southeast-asia other
Southeast Asia is a region of Asia often referenced when describing where cyber activity or victims are located.

Spain is a country in southwestern Europe.

specially crafted input technique

Remote access to a computer using Secure Shell, an encrypted network administration protocol.

static analysis technique

StepSecurity's Harden-Runner is a GitHub Actions security tool that monitors and restricts workflow network and file activity.

stolen accounts concept

stolen credentials concept

stolen data concept

Stored is a ZIP entry type in which file data is saved without compression.
Stored data concept
Stored data is information saved on a device, server, database, or cloud service.

Subdomains are parts of a domain name, such as blog.example.com, that can point to separate websites or services.
subrequests technique

suppliers organization

supply chain concept

surveillance concept

suspicious behavior concept
Suspicious behavior is activity that looks unusual or risky and may suggest fraud or an attack.
system access concept
System access means the ability to log in to or use a computer, application, or network.

tactics concept

taiwan other

takedowns technique

Team PCP is a named group or organization referenced in security reporting.

Changes to computers, software, networks, or other technology systems.

text messages concept

Software, services, or devices supplied by an outside company rather than built by the organization using them.

united-states

also: U.S., The United States, US
